title: How to Manage Short Term Rentals for Maximum Profit
summary: Vacation rental managers grow profitable portfolios by managing short term rentals smarter, not by scaling headcount alone.
body_text: STR management is not passive income. It is a 24/7 hospitality operation, and the operators who scale it successfully are the ones who stop relying on effort alone and start building systems that run without them. Short-term rental management is the active, daily operation of a hospitality business running on real-estate infrastructure. Most operators discover the truth about it the same way: somewhere between their third property and their fifth, the calendar fills up and the chaos begins. Guest messages stack up overnight. A cleaner cancels two hours before checkout. A smart lock battery dies at 11 PM. What looked like a real-estate investment starts running like a hotel front desk, except there is no front desk. The gap between expectation and reality is structural, not accidental. Platforms like Conduit emerged to address what operators running large portfolios consistently describe as the coordination gap no spreadsheet, group chat, or single PMS was architected to close, a problem surfaced repeatedly in operator forums, industry surveys, and Conduit's own 2026 case studies with multi-property operators. Most vacation rental property managers and operations leads assume that consistent, high-quality STR management at scale requires a proportionally larger human team; the best operators can do is hire carefully, build good SOPs, and use a PMS to stay organized. See our AI for hospitality for how this works in practice. Every booking on Airbnb or Vrbo triggers a cascade of time-sensitive tasks: guest screening, pre-arrival communication, turnover coordination, post-stay review requests, and maintenance triage. None of these tasks are optional, and none of them wait for business hours. Short-term rentals can generate 2 to 3 times more gross revenue than long-term rentals for the same property, with separate estimates putting the gross revenue premium at 30 to 80 percent above long-term rental income. But that premium is directly proportional to operational intensity: every additional booking cycle resets guest communication, cleaning, pricing, and maintenance requirements from scratch. More revenue means more repetitions of every task, not a smoother ride. 2 to 3 times More gross revenue than long-term rentals STR management operates across three domains at once. Guest experience covers every touchpoint from inquiry to review response. Property operations covers turnover scheduling, maintenance routing, and smart-home monitoring. Financial and compliance oversight covers dynamic pricing, occupancy tax remittance, and local permit requirements. A failure in one domain cascades into the others: a missed maintenance ticket becomes a guest-facing problem, a guest-facing problem becomes a review, and a damaged review compounds into lower search placement and reduced occupancy. Key takeaways Short-term rental management stops being passive income the moment you hit three to five properties, that's when coordination overhead, not vacancy rate, becomes the real margin killer. Guest communication, cleaning turnover, dynamic pricing, and maintenance are the four operational pillars of every STR business, and none of them can be reliably delegated to luck or a checklist alone. Owning the right tools, a PMS, channel manager, dynamic pricer, smart locks, and running an actually automated operation are two different things; the tools don't talk to each other without a coordination layer in between. Erwan Le Roy ran 35 properties to a 96% automation rate and sub-1-minute response times without adding headcount, the bottleneck wasn't staffing, it was the absence of a system that understood how the business actually ran. The self-manage vs. hire-a-property-manager decision is a margin question, not a lifestyle one, and the math shifts dramatically once you have operational infrastructure that absorbs routine volume. STR permits and zoning compliance aren't a one-time setup task; the regulatory workload compounds with every property you add and varies by jurisdiction. Conduit.ai closes the coordination gap by acting as an AI-powered guest communication layer that makes decisions, answering guests, routing issues, and handling routine volume, so operators scale the portfolio without scaling the headcount. Core Operational Responsibilities in STR Management - The Four Pillars You Can't Outsource to Luck Four operational responsibilities sit at the center of every short-term rental business: guest communication, cleaning turnover, dynamic pricing , and property maintenance. The common assumption is that consistent, high-quality STR management at scale requires a proportionally larger human team; the best operators can do is hire carefully, build good SOPs, and use a PMS to stay organized. In reality, these four responsibilities are not four separate to-do lists. They are a chain, and when one link breaks, the others feel it immediately. One of the clearest patterns we see in early-stage STR operations is that new managers rarely lack effort, they lack structure. When someone steps into a role covering all four pillars at once, guest communication, cleaner scheduling, maintenance coordination, and owner relations, they are effectively on call around the clock with no structural relief. The result is response fatigue, quality degradation, and an operator who becomes the bottleneck rather than the backbone of the business. The sections below address each responsibility directly, including where automation removes the structural pressure before it compounds. "STR managers handling all four core operational pillars, guest communication, cleaner scheduling/checks, maintenance coordination, and owner relations, are effectively on call 24/7 with no structural relief or backup from ownership." 1. Guest Communication Systems - Building Proactive Touchpoints That Prevent 3 AM Panic Messages Response time is no longer just a courtesy metric. Platforms including VRBO have begun surfacing host response times directly to potential guests, making communication speed a visible booking conversion signal , not just a background algorithm input. A guest who waits too long for check-in instructions doesn't just feel frustrated, they write about it. That review drops your score, your score drops your search ranking, and your ranking drops your occupancy. Proactive communication systems break this chain before it starts. This is also where the staffing math breaks down at scale. Running a centralized reservations or guest services team to cover inbound messages across multiple properties and platforms is expensive, and the labor cost scales directly with volume. Conduit's AI Agents are designed specifically to eliminate that bottleneck, handling the round-the-clock communication load that currently requires a human on standby, without proportionally increasing headcount. The agent is most effective when the business already has documentation in place: SOPs, FAQs, house manuals. Once those are connected, the agent can begin handling guest replies within days, and continues operating continuously, before, during, and after every stay. Conduit's Integrations pull from existing content directly, so there is no manual re-entry of information the business has already built. Automated Workflows then handle the predictable touchpoints, booking confirmations, pre-arrival instructions, check-in codes, parking details, house rules, triggered automatically after events like a confirmed reservation or a detected check-in keyword. The goal is to answer the predictable majority of inbound questions before guests think to ask them, freeing your team's attention for the minority that requires genuine judgment. For operators managing communications across multiple platforms or properties simultaneously, the Inbox gives the operations or support team a single place to monitor, review, and manage every conversation the AI agent is handling, so oversight doesn't require jumping between platforms or relying on memory. 2. Turnover Cleaning Standards - Defining the Line Between a Standard Flip and a Deep Clean A standard flip between back-to-back bookings and a deep clean after a long stay are not the same job, and treating them identically is one of the most common sources of guest complaints. When booking patterns compress, three two-night stays in a single week, the margin for a missed detail shrinks to almost nothing. The operational fix is a two-tier checklist: A standard flip protocol for routine turnovers A deep-clean protocol triggered by stay length, guest count, or seasonal transitions Cleaners should not be guessing which standard applies. That ambiguity is where a missed towel or an unreported maintenance issue slips through and surfaces in a guest review instead of a cleaner's report. Cleaner coordination through platforms like Turno is also one of the first responsibilities to degrade when an operator is stretched across all four pillars without delegation infrastructure. When the same person managing guest messages at midnight is also scheduling turnovers at 7 AM, the communication gaps between those tasks are where errors accumulate. Structured turnover workflows, triggered automatically after a checkout event is detected, remove the manual handoff and ensure the right protocol reaches the right person without a manager in the middle of every exchange. 3. Dynamic Pricing Management - Adjusting Nightly Rates Around Seasonality, Demand, and Competitor Data Adjusting nightly rates around seasonality, demand, and competitor data is one of the highest-leverage decisions an STR operator makes. Static pricing is one of the most expensive passive decisions an STR operator can make. Based on our market understanding and PriceLabs' own published operator analyses, active dynamic pricing strategies consistently outperform fixed-rate approaches on revenue per available night, because demand signals, local events, competitor availability, and booking window length shift constantly and a static rate captures none of that upside. Key takeaway: Effective dynamic pricing requires a human review layer for anomalies, not just a tool running on default settings. Effective dynamic pricing requires a human review layer for anomalies, not just a tool running on default settings. 4. Routine Property Inspections - Scheduling Off-Season and Between-Stay Walkthroughs Before Guests Find Problems First Schedule walkthroughs before guests find problems first. A significant share of maintenance issues in short-term rentals are first reported by guests rather than caught during operator inspections. A guest who discovers a broken shower head or a faulty lock doesn't submit a maintenance ticket, they leave a review. Proactive inspection schedules, triggered by stay length and property age, catch those issues before the next guest arrival rather than after the damage to your rating is already done. Maintenance coordination is also the responsibility most likely to fall through the cracks when an operator is absorbing all four pillars without a structural system behind them. When guest communication is consuming the available attention, especially overnight, maintenance flags get delayed, and delayed flags become guest complaints. Routing guest-reported issues through an AI agent that can triage, log, and escalate based on keyword detection keeps those signals from getting buried in a crowded inbox during a high-volume stretch. Technology and Automation Tools Essential to STR Management: and the Coordination Gap They Leave Open The standard short-term rental tech stack is genuinely impressive on paper. A property management system centralizes reservations. A channel manager kills double-bookings. Dynamic pricing fills the calendar. Smart locks remove the front-desk dependency. Together, they look like automation. The problem is that owning the right tools and running an automated operation are two entirely different things. 1. Conduit.ai - Best AI Coordination Layer for Managing Short Term Rentals at Scale The tools above solve data fragmentation; they deliberately leave the coordination problem unsolved. Every handoff between a confirmed booking, a cleaning assignment, an inspection sign-off, and a guest check-in message still requires a human to route, confirm, and act. At 20 or 30 properties, those moments compound into a full-time coordination job that no single point solution was designed to eliminate. Conduit.ai sits above the existing stack as a coordination intelligence layer, most beneficial when operations involve specific brand standards, escalation policies, or complex multi-property workflows that require differentiated behavior across properties. The operator who already owns Hostaway or OwnerRez plus PriceLabs plus smart locks does not need to replace their stack. They need the layer that makes those tools finally talk to each other, a coordination function that Conduit's 2026 case studies show enabled Haven Vacation Rentals to run 270 properties with 2 people per shift, the result of pairing the AI layer with well-documented property policies and clear escalation paths, not a plug-and-play outcome. The tools covered here define the infrastructure floor, the minimum viable stack for managing short-term rentals without constant firefighting. 270 Properties run by just 2 people per shift 2. Channel Managers (Hostfully, Lodgify, Hospitable): Powerful OTA Sync, Blind to On-the-Ground Reality Channel managers synchronize calendars across Airbnb, Vrbo, and direct booking sites in real time, preventing the double-bookings that cost operators both money and reviews. Operators without synchronized OTA calendars face near-certain calendar conflicts at scale, a pattern consistently documented among multi-platform operators managing more than five properties. The hard limit: a channel manager confirms a reservation exists. It cannot confirm the property is guest-ready, the cleaner showed up, or the turnover was completed before the next arrival. 3. PriceLabs - Dynamic Revenue Optimization That Ignores Operational Capacity PriceLabs uses demand signals, local events, and competitor supply to adjust nightly rates algorithmically, and the revenue lift over manual pricing is material. The structural gap is that it optimizes for occupancy with zero awareness of whether your turnover crew can physically execute back-to-back same-day bookings. Aggressive pricing fills nights; it does not coordinate the people required to make those nights deliverable. 4. Smart Locks (Nuki, August, Schlage): Keyless Access Automation With a Verification Blind Spot Smart locks are now table-stakes infrastructure for STR operators. Contactless self-check-in removes front-desk dependency entirely, and enterprise solutions like PointCentral are purpose-built for portfolio-wide smart home management. The verification gap: a smart lock confirms a code was used. It cannot confirm a cleaner completed the turnover before that code fired. Operators running 20-plus properties have learned this the hard way when a guest walks into an uncleaned unit minutes after a code activates on schedule. 5. STR Accounting Tools (REI Hub, VRPlatform): Financial Clarity Without Operational Context Purpose-built STR accounting platforms like REI Hub track rental income, owner payouts, cleaning fees, and expense categorization in ways generic tools like QuickBooks cannot match. For hosts managing short term rentals as investment properties, this financial visibility is essential for tax preparation and profitability analysis. The coordination gap: these tools record what happened financially after the fact but have no connection to the operational workflows, a missed cleaning or a maintenance cost that wasn't logged never surfaces until it's a problem. Related Reading How To Automate Airbnb Business Vrbo Management Airbnb Self Check In Vacation Rental Automation Best Apps For Short Term Rentals Best Pms For Airbnb Best Pms For Short Term Rentals Best Accounting Software For Short Term Rentals How To Manage A Vacation Rental Property Vrbo Smart Pricing Should I Self-Manage or Hire a Property Manager? A Decision Framework Based on Portfolio Size and Margin Goals A Decision Framework Based on Portfolio Size and Margin Goals Deciding between self-managing your short-term rental portfolio and hiring a professional property manager looks like a lifestyle question on the surface. In practice, it is a margin question, and the math changes significantly depending on what operational infrastructure you already have in place. The conventional framing treats this as a binary, self-manage and keep the margin, or delegate and surrender 25–35% of gross revenue, but that framing obscures the real synthesis: both paths converge on the same margin ceiling unless a third coordination layer exists, and the emergence of AI-driven operational infrastructure makes the traditional binary obsolete past roughly ten units. The 3-Property Threshold - Why Self-Management Complexity Compounds Before Revenue Does Self-management works well for one or two properties. At three, the coordination load shifts in a way that catches most operators off guard. The 3-property mark is where scheduling conflicts, guest inquiry volume, and turnover coordination start compressing net income rather than growing it. Operators managing several properties manually often spend a significant number of hours each week on routine tasks alone, and that number climbs steeply with each additional unit. The revenue does not triple when you add a third property, but the operational complexity often does. One of the most common patterns we see with newer operators is a property generating well below what market benchmarks suggest it should be earning: Slow guest inquiry responses that cost bookings Inconsistent pricing that misses demand windows Review scores that drift downward when communication is reactive rather than consistent Each of those is a coordination failure before it is a revenue failure. What Property Managers Actually Charge and What the 15-35% Fee Range Really Buys You According to Vacasa's homeowner guides , full-service operators like Vacasa typically charge between 25% and 35%, while the broader market average for full-service management sits closer to 18–25%. That fee covers listing creation, guest communication, cleaning coordination, and maintenance routing. An independent breakdown published by RedAwning reinforces that the total cost of full-service management frequently reaches the upper end of that range once ancillary fees are factored in. The real question is not whether 25% sounds high, it is whether your current self-management approach is silently costing you more through pricing errors, slow response times, and inconsistent guest experiences that drag down review scores. A property earning well below the local market median is already paying a hidden fee in the form of unrealized revenue; the issue is that fee never appears on an invoice. How to Use AirDNA to Run the Math Before You Decide AirDNA provides market-level benchmarking data, average daily rate, occupancy, and revenue per available night, for specific zip codes and property types. Before committing to a management arrangement, pull the local comp data for your market. If a property manager projects revenue on a property where AirDNA shows the local market median is materially lower, that projection deserves scrutiny. Conversely, if you are self-managing a property where comparable units consistently outperform your current income, the performance gap may justify the management fee, or it may point to a pricing and communication problem a manager alone will not fix. Misaligned management, whether self-directed or outsourced, is the more common culprit behind that gap than the property itself. The Hidden Variable That Changes the Self-Manage vs. Hire Decision - Coordination Infrastructure The real decision variable is not property count or fee percentage; it is what coordination mechanism you install. The critical insight that neither the self-management nor the full-service management camp surfaces is this: manual self-management and full-service management both hit the same margin ceiling when coordination remains a human bottleneck. An AI-driven coordination layer changes the denominator, it absorbs routine volume without adding to the payroll line, which is why the self-manage-versus-hire binary becomes genuinely obsolete past roughly ten units. Conduit's operational model addresses the problem structurally rather than cosmetically. The platform's AI Agents are most beneficial when a business receives a high volume of repetitive guest messages and already has existing documentation, SOPs, FAQs, property manuals, to train the agent on. Once those materials are connected, the agent begins handling automated guest replies within days, not weeks, and operates continuously: before, during, and after a stay, whenever a guest sends a message. That means inquiry response times stop being a function of how many hours an operator has available, which directly protects occupancy and review scores, the two metrics most responsible for the significant performance gaps operators frequently discover too late. The Inbox feature gives the operations team ongoing visibility, allowing them to monitor, review, and manage every conversation the AI agent is handling without becoming the bottleneck in each one. Workflows extend that logic further: after a trigger event, a confirmed booking, a check-in, a detected keyword, automated touchpoints execute without requiring manual staff action, standardizing the guest experience across every property in the portfolio. For operators who already use tools like Notion, Google Drive, or Airbnb, the Integrations layer means the AI agent draws on existing content without requiring manual re-entry, so the operational lift of adding a new property does not scale with headcount. Scale a portfolio without proportionally increasing headcount Maximize revenue per property by improving occupancy and guest satisfaction through consistent communication Standardize brand voice and SOPs across every property and market These are capabilities that neither pure self-management nor traditional full-service management delivers at the same margin. The fee question only resolves cleanly once the coordination question is answered first. Legal and Compliance Requirements for Short-Term Rentals - What You Must Check Before the First Booking Local STR regulations, permits, and zoning laws must be verified before the first booking and monitored continuously afterward. Operating without the required permits exposes hosts to fines, forced delisting, and in some jurisdictions, criminal liability. Compliance is not a setup task; it is a recurring operational workload that grows with every property you add. 1. Local Zoning and Land-Use Permits - Confirm STR Is Allowed Before You List Many hosts discover zoning violations only after receiving a county enforcement letter, sometimes years into operating. When managing short term rentals, verifying that your property's zoning classification explicitly permits STR activity is the single most critical pre-launch step. Some municipalities ban STRs outright in residential zones, others require conditional-use approval. The tradeoff: zoning research is time-consuming and hyper-local, requiring direct contact with municipal planning offices rather than relying on platform guidance. 2. Short-Term Rental Business License and Registration - Secure Your Permit Number Jurisdictions like Virginia Beach have elevated STR violations to criminal offenses, meaning operating without a valid business license or registration number is no longer just a civil fine risk. Hosts managing short term rentals must obtain the correct municipal permit, display the license number in all listings, and renew annually. The key limitation is that license requirements vary dramatically city by city, and platforms like Airbnb do not proactively enforce local registration mandates on your behalf. 3. Lease and HOA Subletting Restrictions - Read Every Clause Before Accepting Guests Airbnb explicitly states that unauthorized subletting is not a violation of its own policies, meaning the platform will continue processing bookings even if your lease or HOA agreement prohibits STR activity entirely. Hosts have faced eviction mid-booking, leaving guests stranded. When managing short term rentals in rented or HOA-governed properties, a thorough review of subletting clauses is non-negotiable. The tradeoff: even a permissive landlord's verbal approval is legally insufficient without written amendment. 4. STR-Specific Insurance Coverage - Don't Rely on Standard Homeowners Policies Standard homeowners insurance policies routinely deny claims when a property is being used as a short-term rental at the time of loss, treating commercial hosting activity as a policy exclusion. Hosts managing short term rentals need a dedicated STR insurance product or a commercial landlord rider that explicitly covers guest-caused damage, liability claims, and loss of rental income. The real tradeoff is cost, purpose-built STR policies carry higher premiums, but the alternative is bearing catastrophic out-of-pocket exposure. 5. Transient Occupancy Tax Registration - Collect and Remit Before Your First Payout Most states and municipalities impose transient occupancy taxes (TOT) or lodging taxes on short-term rental revenue, and failure to register as a tax collector before your first booking creates retroactive liability with penalties and interest. While some platforms auto-collect TOT in select jurisdictions, many markets still require hosts to register independently, file returns, and remit taxes directly to local authorities. The key limitation: tax rules change frequently, and platform auto-collection does not guarantee full local compliance. Best Practices for STR Management at Scale: and the Coordination Layer That Separates 5-Property Operators from 50-Property Operators Scaling from 10 properties to 50 is not a hiring problem dressed up as an operations problem. The operators who cross that threshold without bloating payroll have something structural in place: a coordination layer that absorbs routine volume so humans only touch work that genuinely requires judgment. 1. Conduit.ai - Best for AI-Powered Guest Communication at Scale Airbnb's search ranking is widely understood among operators to reward consistently high review scores, and response lag is one of the most direct ways to erode those scores, a pattern borne out by the experience of operators who have tracked ranking changes alongside communication metrics. At scale, that lag is structural. Human response time degrades as message volume grows; a coordination layer does not. Erwan Le Roy of Cash Flow Street scaled operations using AI for hospitality without adding a single headcount, according to the Conduit case study published in 2026. Haven Vacation Rentals illustrates the same principle at greater scale, achieving a 9-star rating. Jack, Haven's CEO, described adding 14 listings in January with zero new hires. That outcome is only possible when the AI handling guest messages is hospitality-native, not a generic auto-responder retrofitted from another industry. Conduit.ai operates across Airbnb, Vrbo, and direct-book channels simultaneously, handling high-frequency, low-judgment messages that consume most of a team's shift. The honest trade-off: it requires a well-maintained knowledge base to perform at that level. Operators who document property-specific policies and edge cases get compounding returns; those who deploy it with minimal setup will see partial automation, not the 96% ceiling that structured operators reach. 2. Hostaway - Best Central Command Hub for Multi-Platform STR Portfolios Hostaway centralizes reservations, owner statements, and channel synchronization across Airbnb, Vrbo, and direct-book platforms, removing the double-booking risk and calendar chaos that derails multi-platform portfolios. At this stage, it is a non-negotiable infrastructure layer. The limitation surfaces when the PMS is treated as the communication layer too. A PMS routes messages; it does not resolve them. Hostaway is most valuable when paired with a dedicated guest communication layer that handles resolution autonomously, leaving the PMS to consolidate operational data and financial reporting. 3. PriceLabs - Best Dynamic Pricing Engine for Revenue-Focused STR Operators Static pricing is one of the most significant margin leaks in STR portfolios, compounding invisibly. Dynamic-pricing users consistently outperform fixed-rate portfolios on RevPAR, with the performance gap widening most sharply during local-event demand spikes, holidays, and periods of competitor supply change, exactly the moments when a static rate leaves the most money on the table. PriceLabs is most effective when an operator has enough booking history to feed its algorithm meaningful signals, typically after 6 to 12 months of occupancy data per property. 4. Documented SOPs via Yardi Breeze Framework - Best Operational Foundation for Scaling Past 20 Properties The coordination layer that separates 5-property operators from 50-property operators isn't software alone, it's documented standard operating procedures. Using a structured SOP framework ensures that cleaning protocols, maintenance escalation paths, and guest communication standards live in systems, not in one person's head. This approach is essential before hiring your second operations hire. The real limitation: SOPs require disciplined ongoing maintenance; outdated procedures create more confusion than having none at all. 5. Specialized Role Segmentation - Best Organizational Structure for STR Teams Crossing 30+ Units Past 30 units, generalist coordination breaks down. The operators who scale past that threshold without proportionally growing headcount typically segment roles explicitly: a dedicated guest communication function (increasingly AI-handled), a field operations lead who owns cleaner and maintenance vendor relationships, and a revenue manager who owns pricing strategy and channel performance. Blending all three into a single operations role works at 10 properties; it becomes the bottleneck at 40. Start with our AI for hospitality . Platform algorithms now treat response lag as a direct ranking and conversion signal, which means every hour your inbox goes unanswered is simultaneously a booking loss and a review score risk. And as the 270-property Haven Vacation Rentals example shows, the scaling variable between a 5-property and a 50-property operation isn't headcount, it's whether a coordination layer exists that routes, responds, and acts without a human in the middle of every exchange. Together, those two realities point to the same next step: installing something that handles the high-volume, low-judgment communication load before it compounds into a ceiling your PMS and pricing tool can't lift. Start with conduit.ai to see how Conduit handles the guest communication layer your current stack leaves open. Connect your existing SOPs and property documentation, and automated guest replies go live within days. Frequently Asked Questions What does a short-term rental property manager actually do day to day? A short-term rental manager handles the active, daily operation of a hospitality business across three domains simultaneously: guest experience (every touchpoint from inquiry to review response), property operations (turnover scheduling, maintenance routing, and smart-home monitoring), and financial and compliance oversight (dynamic pricing, occupancy tax remittance, and local permit requirements). Every booking triggers a cascade of time-sensitive tasks, guest screening, pre-arrival communication, turnover coordination, post-stay review requests, and maintenance triage, none of which are optional or wait for business hours. At what point does managing my own short-term rentals stop making sense? Industry data consistently points to the 3-property mark as where scheduling conflicts, guest inquiry volume, and turnover coordination start compressing net income rather than growing it. Beyond roughly ten units, the traditional binary of self-managing versus hiring a property manager both converge on the same margin ceiling unless a third coordination layer, such as an AI-driven operational infrastructure, is in place. Does dynamic pricing software handle everything, or do I still need to stay involved? Dynamic pricing tools like PriceLabs use demand signals, local events, and competitor supply to adjust nightly rates algorithmically, and the revenue lift over manual pricing is material. However, the post is clear that effective dynamic pricing still requires a human review layer for anomalies, and tools like PriceLabs optimize for occupancy with zero awareness of whether your turnover crew can physically execute back-to-back same-day bookings. How do I stop guests from messaging me at 3 AM about check-in details? The fix is a proactive communication system that answers predictable questions before guests think to ask them, booking confirmations, pre-arrival instructions, check-in codes, parking details, and house rules, all triggered automatically after events like a confirmed reservation. Conduit.ai's AI Agents and Automated Workflows are designed to handle exactly this round-the-clock communication load, and they work most effectively when you already have SOPs, FAQs, and house manuals documented and connected. What's the difference between a standard flip and a deep clean, and why does it matter? A standard flip between back-to-back bookings and a deep clean after a long stay are not the same job, and treating them identically is one of the most common sources of guest complaints. The operational fix described in the post is a two-tier checklist, a standard flip protocol for routine turnovers and a deep-clean protocol triggered by stay length, guest count, or seasonal transitions, so cleaners are never guessing which standard applies.

title: How Much Money Should You Keep in CDs to Meet Your Goals?
summary: balance savings accounts and CDs to maximize growth, flexibility and keep money for when you need it. Build a strategy that balances returns; security.
body_text: How Much Money Should You Keep in CDs to Meet Your Goals? Share: Copied! Key takeaways: The best savings strategy often combines a savings account and certificates of deposit (CDs) to balance flexibility with long-term growth. Use CDs for money you can leave untouched until the maturity date to earn a guaranteed rate of return. According to Ben Joergens, the right CD allocation depends on your goals, timeline, and liquidity needs—not a one-size-fits-all approach. Certificates of deposit (CDs) can be a simple way to earn a fixed rate of interest on your savings. When you open a CD, you agree to leave your money on deposit for a set period of time – known as the “term” – in exchange for a guaranteed interest rate. Because you're committing to keep your money on deposit, CDs typically offer higher interest rates than traditional savings accounts. In most cases, you'll pay a penalty if you withdraw your money before the CD matures, making CDs best suited for savings you won't need right away. That tradeoff can leave many savers wondering whether a CD is the right place for their savings. While locking in a competitive rate can help your savings grow, you also want to make sure you have enough cash available for your day-to-day life. The good news is that it doesn't have to be an either-or decision. This guide will help you determine how much money to keep in a CD, how much to leave in a savings account, and when each option makes the most sense for your financial goals. Savings Account vs. CD: Which is Right for Your Money? The right mix depends on when you'll need your money. A savings account or high-yield savings account is generally best for your emergency fund and savings you'll need in the near future because it offers easy access to your funds. A CD may be a better choice for savings you can leave untouched until a specific maturity date, since the fixed interest rate usually provides a greater return than a traditional savings account. I often say that it's not necessarily an either-or decision. Savings accounts and CDs often serve different purposes, and many successful savers use both as part of a broader strategy. Rather than asking which account is better, consider how each one can support a different part of your overall savings strategy . How to Decide How Much to Put in a CD There's no one-size-fits-all answer to how much money you should keep in a certificate of deposit. A good rule of thumb is to put only the savings you won't need until the CD matures. One helpful way to think about it is to divide your savings into three categories: emergency savings, near-term needs, and money you can comfortably set aside for longer-term goals. 1. Keep Your Emergency Fund Accessible Before investing in a CD, it's important to have an emergency fund in a savings account or other readily accessible account. Financial experts generally recommend keeping three to six months' worth of essential living expenses set aside for unexpected events, such as a job loss, medical emergency or major home or vehicle repair. Because CDs typically charge an early withdrawal penalty, they're generally not the best place to keep money you may need at a moment's notice. I generally encourage customers to think of savings in layers. Emergency funds should remain accessible, while money earmarked for future goals may be appropriate for CDs. 2. Set Aside Money for Upcoming Expenses Next, think about any expenses you'll need to cover during the life of the CD. If you're planning to buy a car, pay college tuition, renovate your home or take a vacation within the next several months, keeping those funds in an accessible account may provide more flexibility. Matching your savings to your timeline can help you avoid withdrawing money from a CD before it matures. 3. Put the Rest to Work Once you've accounted for your emergency fund and near-term expenses, you may consider putting the remaining savings toward a CD if you won't need the money until the end of its term. With a CD, your money remains on deposit for a fixed term, which can help your savings earn a predictable return. For long-term financial goals, a CD can be a useful way to earn more on money you can afford to leave untouched. Building a CD Strategy After you've decided how much of your savings you're comfortable setting aside, the next step is choosing a CD strategy that aligns with your financial goals and timeline. You can start by thinking about when you'll need the cash. If you're saving for a specific expense, such as a wedding, tuition payment, or home improvement project, choosing a CD with a maturity date that lines up with that goal can help you earn interest while ensuring your funds are available when you need them. If you're saving for a longer-term goal and don't expect to need the money all at once, you don't have to put it into a single CD. Some savers spread their funds across multiple CDs with different maturity dates. This approach, known as CD laddering, can provide more regular access to your savings while still allowing you to take advantage of competitive CD rates. If you're considering this strategy, it's worth learning how CD laddering works and whether it fits your financial goals. It's also a good idea to revisit your savings plan from time to time. A new job, growing family or changing financial priorities may affect how much money you want to keep readily available versus how much you're comfortable setting aside in CDs. Reviewing your savings periodically can help ensure your strategy continues to support both your short-term needs and long-term goals. Find the Right Balance for Your Savings Deciding how much money to keep in a CD comes down to balancing today's needs with tomorrow's goals. By keeping enough savings readily available for emergencies and near-term expenses while setting aside money you won't need right away, you can create a strategy that offers both flexibility and the opportunity to earn more on your savings. I believe the most effective CD strategy is one that supports your goals, maintains appropriate liquidity, and allows you to stay flexible as financial needs evolve. If you're unsure how CDs fit into your overall financial plan, connecting with a personal banker can help. Together, you can build a savings plan that balances accessibility with long-term goals and choose the accounts that best support your financial future. About the Author Ben Joergens is Director of Financial Empowerment at Old National Bank and a Certified Financial Education Instructor with over 26 years of banking experience. As a nationally recognized financial educator, Ben received the ABA George Bailey Distinguished Service Award (2015) and the NFEC Financial Educator of the Year Award (2017). He specializes in helping consumers build financial confidence and achieve their financial goals. In addition, Ben is the host of Old National's Real-Life Finance Podcast which focuses on everyday financial solutions that empower listeners to build the financial future they richly deserve.

title: When Chat GPT Isn't Enough for Building Business Software
summary: ChatGPT can build a working app fast but it doesn't handle permissions, external users, or changing workflows
body_text: AI can build impressive software quickly. Building something your business can safely run on is a different problem. You typed a few sentences into a chat window last week, and by the next morning you had a working app. A login screen, a dashboard, a form that saves to a database. It felt like magic. Then someone on your team asked, "can our customers, partners, and contractors log into this and only see what they're supposed to see?" and the good feeling started to wobble. That question is the whole article. Not "can AI build software?" It clearly can. The real question is: can you actually run your business on what it built? TL;DR ChatGPT (and Claude, Lovable, and similar tools) can genuinely build working software now: interfaces, prototypes, small tools, API connections. That's not in question. The question that matters is what happens after the demo: real users, real data, permissions, external people, approvals, and changing requirements. The hard part isn't getting software to work once. It's making sure the right people can use it safely, the process can change, and the system doesn't depend on one person to keep it running. There's a simple production threshold: if the software touches customers, important business data, or a process the team depends on every day, it's worth thinking beyond the generated code. AI can generate useful pieces of software. A business system needs to handle everything around them: users, data, permissions, workflows, external access, and change over time. Can ChatGPT actually build software now? Yes, and it's worth saying plainly: ChatGPT and tools like it are genuinely good at this. They can generate a working interface, write real code, spin up a prototype in minutes, connect systems and APIs, and solve a specific problem fast. ChatGPT itself is increasingly built around creating interactive apps and connecting to other tools and workflows, not just answering questions. So this isn't an article about ChatGPT falling short. The honest starting point is: ChatGPT can build software. The question is whether what it builds is the right system to run your business on. What's the difference between a demo and a business system? A demo says "look, I built it." A business system says "the team, customers, and partners can rely on it every day." Those are two different bars, and AI-generated software clears the first one far more often than the second. Here's what actually changes between the two: AI prototype Business system Looks right Keeps working when different people use it, data changes, and the unexpected happens One user (you, testing it) Multiple roles, each with different access Test data Real business data, with real consequences if it leaks The happy path Exceptions, edge cases, and things going wrong Built by, and understood by, one person A team can use, manage, and change it without depending on one person An internal demo External users: customers, contractors, partners Basic access (logged in or not) Fine-grained permissions (who sees exactly what) Works today Can change as the business changes, without rebuilding the whole thing Nothing in that right-hand column is exotic. It's just what "the business runs on this" actually requires, once more than one person is using it for real. What questions should you ask before putting AI-built software into production? Before anything AI-built goes live with real users or real data, run it through these 7 questions. Each one is more specific than it first sounds. Question What it's really asking What happens if you skip it 1. Can the right people see the right data? Not just "does it have a login," but can Customer A see only Customer A's records, and nothing that belongs to Customer B Data meant for one customer, team, or partner becomes visible to another 2. What happens when someone leaves? Can their access be revoked cleanly, everywhere, the day they leave Former employees or contractors keep a working login long after they've gone 3. What happens when the workflow changes? Can the person who owns the process change it without turning every adjustment into a development project Every process change turns into a development project, so the process stops changing 4. Can external users safely use it? Customers, contractors, or partners, not just your own team, logging in from outside your organization External access quietly becomes the biggest risk in the system 5. What happens when something goes wrong? Who notices, who can fix it, and is there a fallback while it's broken Nobody notices until a customer complains 6. Could someone else safely take over this system tomorrow? Does the knowledge live in the system, or in the head of the person who built it One person becomes responsible for every fix, change, and problem, and the business is stuck if they leave 7. Can the system grow with the business? More users, more records, more workflows, more roles, more exceptions, without starting over The system that worked at 10 people quietly breaks at 30 None of these questions are about whether ChatGPT is capable. They're about what a piece of software has to hold up under once real people depend on it. What's the hidden cost of AI-built software? AI makes the first version of software dramatically cheaper: the interface, the first working flow, the "look, it does the thing." It doesn't make the work that comes after disappear. It shows up later, in the parts you don't see in the demo, but immediately notice when the system has to support a real business. The hidden work usually includes: defining the underlying data structure properly, authentication, permissions, testing beyond the happy path, deployment, monitoring, ongoing maintenance, handling edge cases, supporting the people using it, and changing the workflow as the business changes. Security is one example of the hidden work. But it's not the only one. A system can have no obvious security flaw and still fail operationally: the wrong person sees the wrong record, nobody knows who owns an exception, a workflow changes and the app needs rebuilding, or the one person who understands it leaves. The real cost isn't just "is the code secure?" It's "can the business depend on this?" There's a second cost that's harder to put a number on: if you're the only person who understands how the generated system actually works, you haven't finished building a tool. You've taken on a new piece of infrastructure that depends on you personally. When is ChatGPT actually enough? This matters just as much as the questions above. AI-generated software is often exactly the right amount of software for: prototypes you're using to test an idea, one-off internal tools with a small number of users and no complex permissions or external access, personal productivity tasks, quick experiments, simple calculators, niche interfaces for a narrow job, validating whether an idea is worth building properly at all, and a throwaway tool to explore an idea before deciding whether it's worth turning into something the team depends on. If that's what you're building, keep using ChatGPT. The goal here isn't fewer AI-generated tools. It's knowing which jobs they're actually built for. How do you know you need something more than AI-generated code? Here's a simple test: if the software touches customers, important business data, or a process your team depends on every day, it's worth thinking beyond the generated code, even if the generated version works today. The more of these you have in the same piece of software (people, important data, permissions, repeatable workflows, and external users), the more you're moving from "a useful tool" to "something the business depends on." That's the point where you need to think beyond whether the AI can build it. You need to think about whether the system can hold up. How do ChatGPT and Noloco work together on production software? AI doesn't have to replace your business software. It can sit inside it. AI is genuinely good at generating, interpreting, classifying, summarizing, and building specific, narrow components. Noloco is built for what surrounds that component: the people using it, the permissions , the data, the workflow, and the access for customers, partners, or contractors, so the whole thing can become a system the business actually relies on. One Noloco customer, Aqil at Pod.fm, builds specific components with AI coding tools and embeds them directly inside a Noloco app , with Noloco handling the login, the permissions, and the data underneath. The AI-built piece stays useful. Noloco handles the parts around it that need to keep working as more people, data, and use cases get added. Final thoughts ChatGPT can build software. That was never really the question. The question is what happens once real people, real data, and real consequences are involved, and whether what got built can hold up to that. Most of the time, the answer isn't "use less AI." It's "put a better system around it." Let AI generate the interface, the component, or the first version. Let the system around it handle the work AI shouldn't have to own: who can see what, where the data lives, what happens next, and how the process changes over time. Frequently asked questions Is AI-generated code inherently insecure? Not inherently, but it isn't automatically secure either. A 2025 Veracode study that tested more than 100 AI models found a large share of generated code samples introduced known security vulnerabilities, and that didn't improve much with newer models. Treat AI-generated code the way you'd treat code from a new, untested contributor: reviewed before it touches real data. Can I use ChatGPT or Claude to build a customer-facing portal? You can use them to build parts of one, like a specific interface or component. Whether the whole portal is safe to launch depends on what handles the login, the permissions, and the data underneath, not on which tool wrote the front-end code. What's the difference between a prototype and a production system? A prototype proves an idea works. A production system proves it keeps working: for multiple users with different access levels, with real data, when something goes wrong, and after the business changes its process six months from now. Do I need a developer to move from an AI prototype to something my business can run on? Not necessarily. Some teams hire developers to harden a prototype. Others use a no-code platform that already handles authentication, permissions, and data structure, and connect their AI-generated components to that instead of rebuilding the foundations from scratch. What happens to my AI-built app if I stop paying for the tool that made it? That depends entirely on the tool and how the app was built. It's worth checking before you rely on it: can you export the code, who owns the data, and what breaks if that specific vendor changes its product or pricing. How do I know if my team has outgrown a vibe-coded tool? A common sign is that one person has become the only one who can safely change it. Other signs: you've started asking "who else can see this," multiple people need different access levels, or a small change now means rebuilding a chunk of the app instead of adjusting a setting. title: Coming This Fall to YouTube: The Official Angels Among Us Docuseries

This fall, we're bringing that journey to audiences everywhere with Angels Among Us, an all-new docuseries streaming exclusively on YouTube. The series follows a group of women as they pursue the opportunity of a lifetime: becoming the newest Victoria's Secret Angel and walking the Victoria's Secret Fashion Show runway. title: Immunic Appoints Elena Ridloff to Board of Directors
summary: – Appointment Strengthens Board with Financial, Capital Markets and Commercial Leadership Expertise as the Company Approaches Pivotal Phase 3 ENSURE Readout in Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis as...
body_text: News Releases Immunic Appoints Elena Ridloff to Board of Directors Print Page Email Page PDF Download RSS Feed – Appointment Strengthens Board with Financial, Capital Markets and Commercial Leadership Expertise as the Company Approaches Pivotal Phase 3 ENSURE Readout in Relapsing Multiple Sclerosis as well as Potential Regulatory Filings and Commercialization – NEW YORK , Aug. 10, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Immunic , Inc. (Nasdaq: IMUX), a late-stage biotechnology company pioneering the development of novel oral therapies for neurologic diseases, today announced the appointment of Elena Ridloff, CFA to its Board of Directors, effective August 6, 2026. Ms. Ridloff brings more than two decades of experience driving financial strategy, corporate growth, and capital markets execution across the biopharmaceutical industry. "We are excited to welcome Elena to our Board as we enter an important period for Immunic," commented Michael W. Bonney, Chair of Immunic's Board of Directors. "Ms. Ridloff is a highly respected biotech executive with a proven track record of helping companies navigate periods of transformational growth. We are delighted to welcome her to the Board and look forward to the valuable insights and perspectives she will bring." Erik Lundgren, Chief Executive Officer of Immunic, added, "With top-line data from our Phase 3 ENSURE trials of vidofludimus calcium in relapsing multiple sclerosis (MS) expected by year-end and the planned initiation of our confirmatory Phase 3 program in progressive MS, we are executing towards a series of milestones that have the potential to define Immunic's next phase of growth. Elena's experience building and advising high-growth biopharma companies will be invaluable as we continue to unlock vidofludimus calcium's potential across MS patient populations. I look forward to working closely with her as we move into this next phase." Ms. Ridloff brings more than 20 years of leadership experience in finance, corporate development, investor relations, and capital markets across the biopharmaceutical industry. She currently serves as Chief Financial Officer at Sionna Therapeutics. Previously, Ms. Ridloff served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of ACADIA Pharmaceuticals, where she led the finance organization and played a key role in the company's commercial growth, business development, pipeline expansion, and successfully raising $600 million in capital. Earlier in her career, she established and led the investor relations function at Alexion Pharmaceuticals, was Chief Executive Officer of BIOVISIO, an independent consulting firm serving the life sciences industry, and served as a Managing Director at Maverick Capital, a hedge fund, leading healthcare and life sciences investments. Ms. Ridloff also serves on the Board of Directors of Kymera Therapeutics, where she chairs the Audit Committee, and previously served on the Board of Directors of Kronos Bio. She holds a B.A. in History and Sociology of Science from the University of Pennsylvania and is a CFA charterholder. "I am honored to join Immunic's Board at such an exciting stage in the company's evolution," said Ms. Ridloff. "Immunic has assembled an exceptional team with deep expertise in MS and is advancing a differentiated oral program designed with the potential to become a meaningful franchise opportunity spanning both relapsing and progressive forms of MS. With important clinical milestones ahead, I look forward to working alongside the Board and management team to help advance vidofludimus calcium and support the successful execution of the company's long-term strategy." About Immunic, Inc. Immunic, Inc. (Nasdaq: IMUX) is a late-stage biotechnology company pioneering the development of novel oral therapies for neurologic diseases. The company's lead development program, vidofludimus calcium (IMU-838), is currently being evaluated in Phase 3 clinical trials for the treatment of relapsing multiple sclerosis, with top-line data expected to be available by the end of 2026. Initiation of an additional Phase 3 clinical trial in progressive MS is expected later in 2026. Vidofludimus calcium has already shown therapeutic potential and a favorable safety and tolerability profile in Phase 2 clinical trials in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, progressive multiple sclerosis and other diseases. Vidofludimus calcium combines neuroprotective effects, through its mechanism as a first-in-class nuclear receptor-related 1 (Nurr1) activator, with additional anti-inflammatory and anti-viral effects, by selectively inhibiting the enzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH). The company's development pipeline also includes earlier-stage programs, including IMU-381 and IMU-856, aimed at building a broader therapeutics platform addressing neurodegenerative and autoimmune diseases. For further information, please visit: www.imux.com . title: PepsiCo expands its presence at Silverstone and Formula 1® as momentum accelerates
summary: A new partnership with Silverstone and a record-setting FORMULA 1 PIRELLI BRITISH GRAND PRIX 2026 highlight PepsiCo's growing role at the intersection of sport, entertainment, and fandom.
body_text: The collaboration was part of PepsiCo’s multiyear global partnership with Formula 1® and the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS Formula 1® Team. The partnerships, which kicked off earlier this year, unite PepsiCo’s powerhouse food and beverage brands with these global icons, putting them front and center in a sport at the intersection of performance, entertainment, and culture. Building on Formula 1®'s explosive trajectory — its fanbase grew to 827 million people in 2025 — it places PepsiCo at the heart of the sport's global momentum. Across the season, PepsiCo’s brands are showing up in ways that connect performance, energy, and fan culture. Earlier in the season, STING Energy® brought the sound and speed of Formula 1® to life through its collaboration with DJ Alan Walker recently at the FORMULA 1 MSC CRUISES GRAN PREMIO DE BARCELONA-CATALUNYA 2026. Thousands of fans saw the live debut of the new F1 inspired track that was dropped at the grand prix. Gatorade and the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI) supported hydration in the paddock, including GSSI’s work with drivers like F1 ACADEMY’s Lisa Billard to create bespoke hydration strategies. The team worked with Lisa Billard throughout race weekend conducting hydration and sweat testing during the F1 ACADEMY™ Silverstone Race. The team previously conducted sweat and hydration testing with Billard at the F1 ACADEMY™ Silverstone Test earlier this year and sent personalized hydration and nutrition strategies to help stay hydrated over the race weekend. GSSI has also conducted sweat testing with Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS Formula 1® Team drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, extending its performance science support across the team. Doritos tapped into the bold, high-energy side of Formula 1® through its Taste the Thrill campaign, while Doritos Loaded activations brought fans closer to the action at Silverstone through an interactive, flavor-driven experience, offering fans a chance to win prizes like exclusive merchandise. Gatorade hits the track Fans who’ve dreamed of setting foot on a Formula 1® track got their chance at Silverstone — on their own two feet — with Run the Circuit, where hundreds of participants literally ran the track. Gatorade helped hype up and hydrate participants with a live DJ, branded medals, prizes, F1 ACADEMY™ gear and samples from a massive 3-meter-tall electrolyte dispensing bottle. The GSSI, which brings together top researchers to study athlete performance through hydration and nutrition science, brought their expertise to Run the Circuit, with a pre-run briefing highlighting the importance of being properly hydrated before the race begins, with Gatorade Hydration Booster on hand as the pre-race fuel. Participants received personalized insights into their performance, including sweat rate, electrolyte loss, and hydration needs based on real-time GSSI testing. Additionally, some participants used “dehydration goggles” to see for themselves the negative impact dehydration has on the body — and the importance of proper hydration. Pepsi champions fandom and sustainability Pepsi also brought its new House of Treats platform to Silverstone, giving fans a more experiential way to enjoy Pepsi through crafted, customizable beverages and a diverse menu of crafted drinks spanning distinct flavor profiles, from indulgent and refreshing to sensorial and innovative, including unexpected serves. The brand highlighted sustainability at the race, giving F1® attendees the chance to win prizes if they return their cans and compostable cups at a dedicated vending machine in the fanzone. Those prizes included free Pepsi drinks and branded merchandise like phone straps, as well as Silverstone vouchers and tickets to the FORMULA 1 PIRELLI BRITISH GRAND PRIX 2027.

title: China COVID-19 Summer Wave Intensifies as Infection Rates Climb Above 20 Percent
summary: Rising COVID Cases in China Trigger Fresh Health Concerns Amid New Summer Surge China is facing a renewed wave of COVID-19 infections as official surveillance data shows a sharp increase in positive cases during the summer months.
