According to data released on July 30 by the Chinese Center for Disease Contr
body_text: Rising COVID Cases in China Trigger Fresh Health Concerns Amid New Summer Surge China is facing a renewed wave of COVID-19 infections as official surveillance data shows a sharp increase in positive cases during the summer months. The country’s COVID-19 positivity rate has crossed the 20 percent mark for the first time this year, raising concerns among health experts and the public about another significant outbreak. According to data released on July 30 by the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC), COVID-19 positivity rates reached 20.3 percent between July 20 and July 26. This represents a major increase compared with three weeks earlier, when the positivity rate was recorded at 9.6 percent. The latest figures come from China’s national acute respiratory infection sentinel surveillance system, which monitors trends in respiratory illnesses across the country. The data indicates that COVID-19 has become one of the leading detected infections across multiple age groups. Health authorities reported that southern provinces experienced higher positive detection rates compared with northern regions. The dominant circulating strain identified in the latest surveillance period was the NB.1.8.1 variant lineage, a newer descendant within the Omicron family of variants. Public Reports Point to Growing Infections Across Chinese Cities While official data provides some insight into the current situation, reports from residents across China suggest that infections may be spreading widely in several regions. Social media users from cities including Shanghai, Beijing, Hangzhou, and areas of Shanxi have shared personal accounts of testing positive for COVID-19. Some residents have reported entire households becoming infected, indicating that transmission may be occurring rapidly within communities. A Shanghai resident described experiencing a severe illness during the latest wave, saying symptoms included fever, digestive problems, intense throat pain, coughing, and vomiting. The individual also reported that hospitals were crowded, with long waiting times for medical consultations. The reports have increased public discussion about the severity of the current wave and whether healthcare systems in certain regions may face additional pressure if cases continue rising. Doctors Warn of Increased Pressure on Hospitals Medical professionals in China have also commented on the recent increase in COVID-19 cases. On July 31, a traditional Chinese medicine doctor posted on social media that COVID-19 had returned strongly. Another doctor in Shandong reportedly described crowded emergency departments and limited availability of hospital beds, highlighting concerns about healthcare capacity during periods of increased infection. Although individual reports do not represent nationwide conditions, they reflect growing anxiety among some communities as more people report illness and seek medical care. Taiwan Also Sees COVID-19 Cases Increase The rise in COVID-19 activity is not limited to mainland China. Taiwan has also reported an increase in infections and severe cases. According to surveillance information released by Taiwan’s Centers for Disease Control, COVID-19 related outpatient and emergency visits increased significantly during the latest reporting period. The country recorded 18,990 COVID-related medical visits in one week, representing a 74.8 percent increase compared with the previous week. Taiwan also reported 62 new severe domestic COVID-19 cases in a single week, marking the highest weekly total recorded in 2026. Unlike mainland China, where NB.1.8.1 remains the leading reported lineage, Taiwan’s recent infections have mainly involved the PQ.16.1.1 sublineage. This strain is derived from NB.1.8.1 and belongs to the broader Omicron family. Taiwan health officials have emphasized that vaccination continues to provide protection, particularly in reducing the risk of severe disease and hospitalization. Questions Remain About COVID-19 Tracking and Transparency The latest increase in infections has also renewed discussions about COVID-19 reporting and transparency. Critics have previously questioned whether official infection numbers from China fully represent the scale of outbreaks due to concerns about data availability and reporting practices. Because COVID-19 surveillance methods differ between countries, comparing infection levels directly can be challenging. Official statistics, hospital reports, and community experiences may each provide different views of the overall situation. Health experts continue to recommend monitoring hospitalization rates, severe illness numbers, vaccination coverage, and emerging variants rather than relying only on case counts. Scientists Continue Debate Over COVID-19 Origins At the same time, discussion about the origins of COVID-19 continues among researchers and policymakers worldwide. Dr. Ashish Jha, former White House COVID-19 Response Coordinator under the Biden administration, recently stated that he believes a laboratory-related incident remains the most likely explanation for the pandemic’s origin. He made the comments during an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” program on August 2. Jha said that no one in the United States knows the origin of the virus with certainty and called for additional transparency and accountability regarding available information. The scientific community remains divided on the issue, with different researchers supporting different explanations based on available evidence. What the New Summer Surge Means for Global Health The latest COVID-19 increase in China highlights that the virus continues to evolve and circulate more than six years after the beginning of the pandemic. Although many countries have moved away from emergency pandemic measures, seasonal surges and new variants remain important public health concerns. Experts say continued surveillance, vaccination efforts, access to medical care, and transparent reporting remain essential tools for managing future waves. For individuals, health professionals generally recommend staying aware of local infection trends, following public health guidance, and taking precautions when respiratory illnesses are increasing. The current summer surge in China serves as another reminder that COVID-19 remains an ongoing global health challenge. While the severity of future waves may vary, monitoring new variants and maintaining preparedness will continue to play an important role in protecting communities. Source The Epoch Times, including information attributed to the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Taiwan Centers for Disease Control, and public statements from medical professionals and health experts. Disclaimer This article is intended for informational purposes only and does not provide medical advice. COVID-19 conditions, infection rates, and health recommendations can change over time. Readers should consult qualified healthcare professionals and official public health authorities for the latest guidance related to COVID-19 prevention, vaccination, and treatment.

title: 4 in 5 buyers never join your calls (and three more buying trends from 637 B2B deals)
summary: ‍Analysis based on 2,021 recorded sales conversations across 637 active and closed mid-market and enterprise B2B software deals.
body_text: Ask Sales about a deal's buying committee and they'll point to a CRM record with 20+ contacts. Ask them who actually showed up on calls? Two people. Maybe three. And the person with budget authority almost certainly wasn't one of them. Based on an analysis of 2,021 recorded sales conversations and 637 active and closed mid-market and enterprise deals, here are some interesting learnings about how B2B buying decisions are made today (and why furnishing your champions with the right assets matters more than ever). The sales call is the smallest part of the deal I went into this analysis expecting to learn about who sits on a buying committee. Instead, what I found is that the call is one of the least representative surfaces of a B2B deal. The average buying account has about 23 known contacts in the CRM (median: 10). The average number of people who actually appear on a call is 2.3. Roughly one in five known contacts ever joins a call. In some cuts, this figure is as few as one in eight. The remaining 75–80%? They're cc'd on emails, forwarded internal summaries, or pulled in as end-users after the contract is signed. Some of them have veto power. None have ever heard your pitch. They're reading forwarded summaries, weighing in on Slack threads, sending requirements back through your champion, running the security review, approving the budget (or quietly refusing to). And it isn't only that most of the committee never gets invited. Plenty are invited and don't come. Across the 2,021 calls, buyers' own teams put 6,187 people on invitations. Only 4,547 turned up (73%). This means that roughly one in four invitations went unused. These weren't people who'd left the deal. They'd just stopped using calls to participate in it. All this to say: none of this makes the sales call unimportant . It makes it partial. The call is where you meet the deal but it isn't where the deal gets decided. Trend #1: Self-service buyers are the new normal (and they arrive semi-decided) Across the dataset, Discovery calls consistently involve just 1–2 people (almost always a single end user who has self-identified the pain and initiated contact independently), often without explicit budget authority. Another recurring pattern: multiple champions had already evaluated a direct competitor before their first call. Rather than exploring, they were validating a thesis they'd already formed. This showed up unprompted, at the very opening of first calls, across multiple deals: "Just to be fully transparent, I've looked at Competitor A, Competitor B, there's a few others that I'm going to be looking at over the next couple of weeks." - Marketing lead at an enterprise SaaS company, unprompted at the start of their first demo call This isn't a one-off; it appears consistently enough across the 637-deal set to represent a structural shift: the research phase now happens before the vendor knows the deal exists. Which means the most consequential part of your funnel is the part you have no presence in. What this means for you Discovery is no longer an exploratory conversation; it's a validation meeting. Your champion arrived with a point of view. The job in that first call isn't just to educate but to confirm their thesis and arm them with the language to sell it internally. The question to answer isn't "what problem are you solving?" It's "what do you need to walk away with so you can get your team on board?" But the deeper implication is about the window before that call. If buyers are forming their shortlist while browsing anonymously, the only assets that can influence that stage are the ones that work without a rep in the room. This is the gap interactive demos were built for, and the reason we’re building RepX (conversational sales agents that qualify and convert visitors before a meeting exists). RepX asks the discovery questions a rep would ask, handles competitor and pricing objections, presents a live interactive demo inside the conversation, and books the meeting at the right moment. An early RepX customer told us that their agent handles about 80% of the very specific product questions they get. The point isn't automation for its own sake. It's that the champion in the quotes above was comparing three vendors before speaking to any of them. Whoever answered their questions in that window shaped the shortlist. Trend #2: Economic buyers shape deals without ever joining a call At every stage, CMOs, VPs and SVPs are largely absent from calls. But the trial-stage analysis surfaces a more actionable pattern: champions are actively building internal resources (demos, decks, etc) specifically to pitch leadership. Not just for evaluation, but as their internal business case. Here’s an anonymous extract from one of our own buyers from a recent sales conversation: "I can spend a bit of time trying to polish an example demo and then I can probably get at least one person from each of our teams — sales, engineering and customer success — to maybe get on a call with the two of us…and then if no one is objecting to it, I can use that as data to pitch it to my SVP." - Head of Marketing at a mid-market SaaS company, solo on a working session call The budget owner's name surfaces in these conversations. Their requirements shape what the champion asks for. Their timeline drives urgency. In other words, what they have to work with when you’re not in the room is just as (if not more) important than on-call conversations. What this means for you You're not selling to one person. You're selling through one person into a room you'll never enter. Which reframes the job: your champion isn't a contact to be worked. They're a colleague running an internal campaign on your behalf, usually with no training, no materials and no budget. So the question stops being "how do I get the economic buyer on a call?". Our data says you mostly won't. Instead, it becomes "what am I putting in my champion's hands, and can I see what happens to it?" Both halves of that matter, and the second is the one most teams miss. A slide deck emailed to a champion disappears. You don't know if it was opened, forwarded, or ignored, or who else saw it. That blindness is precisely why the deal record names 2.6 people: calls are the only telemetry most sales teams have, so calls become the only stakeholders they can name. This is what Hubs was built for. A Hub is a single personalized link that holds everything the committee needs (interactive demos, videos, pricing PDFs, ROI material, forms ) laid out either as a gallery to explore or a playlist that walks a buyer through a sequence. Content can be segmented by role, pain point or persona, so the SVP who opens it lands on business impact while an end user lands on workflow. Two things follow from that, and they map directly onto the findings above: It travels where you can't. A hub link is the thing a champion forwards into the internal review you're not invited to. Instead of your argument being reconstructed from memory in a Slack thread, the committee sees the product itself. It gives you telemetry that calls can't. Hubs track who engaged, with what, and how deeply, and push those insights into HubSpot and Slack. That's how a stakeholder who will never join a call becomes a name you can see as well as how "we're multi-threaded" turns from a claim into something your CRM can actually evidence. If you're not actively helping your champion build the internal pitch and watching what happens when they run it, you're leaving the most important conversation in the deal entirely to chance. Trend #3: The people who can kill your deal have never heard your pitch Attendance remains largely consistent through evaluation: Demo → POC → POC complete averages 2.52 → 2.56 → 3.00 prospects per call. Interestingly, however, attendance during procurement collapses to 1.89, with a median of 1. The champion really does walk into the last mile alone. Procurement, Legal, InfoSec and Finance appear in emails for the first time at contract stage. Not during evaluation. Not during trial. At contract. These roles almost never attend a demo or trial call. By the time they enter the picture, they have no context, no relationship and no stake in the outcome. Only the authority to slow things down (or worse). What this means for you The people who can kill your deal are being introduced to your product through a second-hand summary written by a champion who may not know what Legal or InfoSec actually needs to hear. Pre-empt it. In trial, ask your champion directly: "Who else will need to sign off, and what do they need from us?" The earlier you surface these stakeholders, the less power they have to stall. Then make the answer easy to act on. Security documentation, your SOC 2 report, a standard MSA and a short data-flow overview should already be sitting in the Hub you gave your champion in week one in a section addressed to reviewers, framed as partnership transparency rather than a compliance chore. Every question procurement would have asked, answered before they ask it, is a week back in your cycle. And crucially, it isn't your champion who has to go and get it. The same role-segmentation that serves an SVP a business case serves an InfoSec reviewer a security posture. It's the same link. They just land in different places. What this all adds up to If there's one thing to take from 2,021 calls, it's this: we have been measuring the part of the deal that is easiest to see, and mistaking it for the part that matters. The call is a sliver of the decision making process. Half the time it's one person. A quarter of the invitations buyers send their own colleagues go unused. The committee never appears in the CRM. And the decisive conversations (the internal pitch, the security review, the budget approval) all happen somewhere you have no presence and no visibility. The instinct is to fight this: get more people on calls, push for the exec meeting, insist on multi-threading. Our data suggests that's mostly swimming upstream. Buyers aren't withholding attendance out of bad faith. They're doing what every one of us does: evaluating software asynchronously, on their own time, in their own tools, and looping in colleagues by forwarding something rather than booking something. The teams that will win aren't the ones who drag more stakeholders onto Zoom. They're the ones who accept that most of the buying happens without them, and who equip the one person who is there to carry the deal through rooms they'll never enter with product and resources they can show rather than claims they must repeat, and with enough visibility on the other side that the invisible committee stops being invisible.

title: BD Reports Third Quarter Fiscal 2026 Financial Results
summary: Revenue of $5.0 billion increased 5.4% as reported, 4.4% FXN GAAP and adjusted diluted EPS from continuing operations of $1.64 and $3.23, respectively Year-to-date cash from continuing operations...
body_text: Revenue of $5.0 billion increased 5.4% as reported, 4.4% FXN GAAP and adjusted diluted EPS from continuing operations of $1.64 and $3.23, respectively Year-to-date cash from continuing operations increased 33.3% to $2.1 billion and free cash flow increased 44.6% to $1.7 billion Company updates full-year guidance to reflect ongoing momentum, expects revenue growth toward the high end of its range and raises midpoint of adjusted diluted EPS guidance FRANKLIN LAKES, N.J. , Aug. 6, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- BD (Becton, Dickinson and Company) (NYSE: BDX), a leading global medical technology company, today announced results for its fiscal 2026 third quarter, which ended June 30, 2026. "We delivered a strong third quarter, with revenue, adjusted operating margin and adjusted EPS all ahead of our expectations," said Tom Polen, chairman, CEO and president of BD. "Our first full quarter as New BD demonstrates the early benefits of a more focused MedTech company, with strong momentum across our key growth platforms, continued innovation and further progress through BD Excellence. We remain focused on disciplined execution, advancing our key growth platforms, expanding margins and allocating capital strategically to drive sustainable growth and long-term shareholder value." Recent Business Highlights Medical Essentials: Awarded a Vizient Innovative Technology contract for the BD® CentroVena One™ Insertion System , validating CentroVena One ™ Insertion System as a breakthrough innovation designed to simplify central line insertion and enhance patient and clinician safety. BioPharma Systems: Announced a collaboration with EMS, one of Brazil's leading pharmaceutical companies, to expand access to GLP-1 therapies through a semaglutide launch utilizing BD's Vystra™ Injection Pen platform to support consistent, reliable self-injection for patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Interventional: Launched the Elyra™ Thulium Fiber Laser System , expanding BD's kidney stone care portfolio with a system designed to help urology teams enhance efficiency, versatility and procedural workflow. BD named to TIME's 2026 List of America's Best Companies . BD issued its Fiscal Year 2025 Together We Advance Corporate Sustainability Report . Basis of Presentation— Continuing Operations On February 9, 2026, the company completed the spin-off of BD's former Biosciences and Diagnostic Solutions business and the combination of the business with Waters Corporation ("Waters"). The historical results of the former Biosciences and Diagnostic Solutions business, which was previously the Life Sciences segment, are reflected as discontinued operations for all periods presented. Financial information presented in this release reflects BD's results on a continuing operations basis. Prior periods have been recast to conform to this presentation. Such items could have a material impact on GAAP measures of BD's financial performance. A confirmation number is not needed to access the replay. Non-GAAP Financial Measures/Financial Tables This press release contains certain non-GAAP financial measures. These include revenue growth rates on a currency-neutral basis, adjusted diluted earnings per share and free cash flow. These non-GAAP financial measures are not in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States. BD management believes that the use of non-GAAP measures to adjust for items that are considered by management to be outside of BD's underlying operational results or that affect period-to-period comparability helps investors to gain a better understanding of our performance year-over-year, to analyze underlying trends in our businesses, to analyze our operating results, and to understand future prospects. Management uses these non-GAAP financial measures to measure and forecast the company's performance, especially when comparing such results to previous periods or forecasts. We believe presenting such adjusted metrics provides investors with greater transparency to the information used by BD management for its operational decision-making and for comparison to other companies within the medical technology industry. Although BD's management believes non-GAAP results are useful in evaluating the performance of its business, its reliance on these measures is limited since items excluded from such measures may have a material impact on BD's net income, earnings per share or cash flows calculated in accordance with GAAP. Therefore, management typically uses non-GAAP results in conjunction with GAAP results to address these limitations. BD strongly encourages investors to review its consolidated financial statements and publicly filed reports in their entirety and cautions investors that the non-GAAP measures used by BD may differ from similar measures used by other companies, even when similar terms are used to identify such measures. Non-GAAP measures should not be considered replacements for, and should be read together with, the most comparable GAAP financial measures. We present adjusted diluted earnings per share for the third quarter and the first nine months of fiscal year 2026, and the corresponding prior periods, after eliminating items we believe are not part of our ordinary operations and affect the comparability of the periods presented. Adjusted diluted earnings per share includes adjustments for the impact of purchase accounting adjustments, integration and restructuring costs, transaction costs, separation-related costs, certain product remediation costs, certain legal matters, certain investment gains and losses, certain asset impairment charges, certain pension settlement costs, and the impact of the extinguishment of debt. We also present revenue growth rates for the third quarter and the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 over the corresponding prior periods on a currency-neutral basis after eliminating the effect of foreign currency translation, where applicable. We also show the growth in adjusted diluted earnings per share compared to the prior year periods after eliminating the impact of foreign currency translation to further enable investors to evaluate BD's underlying earnings performance compared to the prior period. We calculate foreign currency-neutral percentages by converting our current-period local currency financial results using the prior period foreign currency exchange rates and comparing these adjusted amounts to our current-period results. As exchange rates are an important factor in understanding period-to-period comparisons, we believe the presentation of results on a foreign currency-neutral basis in addition to reported results helps improve investors' ability to understand our operating results and evaluate our performance in comparison to the prior periods. We also present free cash flow for the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 over the corresponding prior period, which is net cash provided by continuing operating activities less capital expenditures, to provide a view of the Company's ability to generate cash for use in acquisitions and other investing and financing activities. Free cash flow is not a measure of cash available for discretionary expenditures given that we have certain non-discretionary obligations such as debt service that are not deducted from the measure. We believe the presentation of results of free cash flow in addition to reported results helps improve investors' ability to understand our operating results and evaluate our performance in comparison to the prior period. New BD refers to BD post the separation of the Biosciences and Diagnostic Solutions business from BD. Reconciliations of these and other non-GAAP measures to the comparable GAAP measures are included in the attached financial tables. Within the attached financial tables presented, certain columns and rows may not add due to the use of rounded numbers. Percentages and earnings per share amounts presented are calculated from the underlying amounts. About BD BD is one of the world's largest pure-play medical technology companies with a Purpose of advancing the world of health™ by driving innovation across medical essentials, connected care, biopharma systems and interventional. The company supports those on the frontlines of healthcare by developing transformative technologies, services and solutions that optimize clinical operations and improve care for patients. Operating across the globe, with more than 60,000 employees, BD delivers billions of products annually that have a positive impact on global healthcare. By working in close collaboration with customers, BD can help enhance outcomes, lower costs, increase clinical efficiency, improve safety and expand access to healthcare. title: 2026 Buick Envista Pricing, Specs, and Release Date
summary: Buick's smallest crossover, the front-wheel-drive Envista, returns for 2026 with its three-cylinder engine and fewer standard features than last year.
body_text: The Buick Envista is a subcompact crossover SUV that hints at a premium experience above its mainstream competitors. Competitors include the Hyundai Kona, Kia Seltos, and Mazda CX-30. 2026 Buick Envista Pricing, Specs, and Release Date What’s New for the 2026 Buick Envista Design Powertrain Interior Technology Safety Pricing and Release Date Further Research What’s New for the 2026 Buick Envista The Buick Envista was introduced for the 2024 model year and has seen few changes since then. That tracks for 2026, with one shade of red exterior paint swapped out for another. Buick has also cut the first aid kit, cargo organizer, and premium floor mats from the standard features list. Design The Envista is a subcompact crossover with a somewhat misleading sporty profile. The tapered nose and raked roofline look great from the side, but hint at a better-performing vehicle than the Envista actually is. Furthermore, the roofline cuts into the second-row passengers’ headroom. The Envista comes standard with 17-inch alloy wheels, and it’s available with 18- and 19-inch wheel designs. The top Avenir trim swaps black exterior trim for body-color trim and side mirrors. Powertrain Every Envista is equipped with a modest turbocharged three-cylinder engine that makes 137 horsepower and 162 pounds-feet of torque. Front-wheel drive (FWD) comes standard, and unlike some options in the class, all-wheel drive (AWD) is not available. A six-speed automatic transmission also comes standard. Driving dynamics are reasonably athletic, though the Envista isn’t particularly powerful. The Envista’s fuel economy ratings are about average for the segment, with ratings of 28 mpg in the city, 32 mpg highway, and 30 mpg combined. Interior The Envista seats five passengers across its two rows. The front seats are comfortable, and the second row has adequate leg room but, again, scant head room. Standard features include manually adjustable front seats with cloth and synthetic leather upholstery. Options include a moonroof, synthetic leather upholstery, black upholstery with tan stitching, a power-adjustable driver’s seat, heated front seats, and a hands-free power liftgate. The Envista’s cargo space is just about average, measuring 20.7 cubic feet behind the second row and a maximum of 42 cubic feet with the second row folded down. Technology Tech features are simple, with most coming standard across the Envista lineup. The Buick Envista features an 8-inch digital instrument display, an 11-inch touch screen infotainment display, wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, and a six-speaker audio system. There are few options or upgrades on the menu, but wireless device charging is available. Search for Buick Envista See all 2025 Buick Envista $23,606 5,808 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Frankfort, IL 2025 Buick Envista $25,789 14,934 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Columbia, IL 2025 Buick Envista $24,995 1,295 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Simi Valley, CA 2025 Buick Envista $21,188 19,429 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Seffner, FL 2025 Buick Envista $23,738 16,712 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Independence, MO 2025 Buick Envista $22,076 12,364 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Clovis, CA Safety The Buick Envista comes standard with a rearview camera, forward-collision warning, forward automatic emergency braking, pedestrian detection, lane-keep assist, lane-departure warning, a rear-seat alert system, General Motors’ Teen Driver safety settings system, and a system that requires seatbelts to be buckled to drive. Options include adaptive cruise control, blind-spot monitoring, and rear cross-traffic alert, but the Envista isn’t available with some of Buick’s more desirable safety features, like the Super Cruise semi-autonomous driving system. In Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) testing, the Envista earned top Good scores in the side and small overlap front evaluations, but the moderate overlap front evaluation yielded the lowest Poor rating. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) hasn’t crash-tested the 2026 Envista, but an early test of the 2025 Envista yielded an overall rating of four out of five stars. Pricing and Release Date The 2026 Buick Envista is available now, in Preferred, Sport Touring, and Avenir trims. As of this writing, the Envista starts at $24,700, moves up to the Sport Touring for $26,200, and starts at $29,500 for the Avenir. These prices do not include the Envista's $1,795 destination fee. title: ​​​​Great Britain leads Europe’s FMCG inflation as NIQ launches new Inflation Barometer
summary: A monthly outlook on FMCG inflation, shopper response, and volume impact in Western Europe. Discover the August Edition.
body_text: Press Releases Print Share London, August 6, 2026: NIQ (NYSE: NIQ) today launches its new EU5 FMCG Inflation Barometer – a monthly tracker across five Western Europe markets – France, Great Britain, Germany, Italy and Spain – designed to help retailers, manufacturers and the media understand how inflation is evolving across Europe’s largest grocery markets and how shoppers are responding. The first edition of the Barometer reveals that while inflation across Europe’s FMCG sector remains relatively contained overall, significant differences persist between countries. Key Findings: Great Britain recorded the highest FMCG inflation across the EU5 at +2.3%1, above the European average of +1.1%. France and Italy reported the lowest inflation at -0.4% and +0.6% retrospectively, highlighting the uneven inflationary landscape across Europe’s major economies The monthly Barometer also tracks department-level inflation, price elasticity, and how shoppers are reacting to inflation to manage higher grocery costs, including buying more on promotion, switching to cheaper products or reducing purchase volumes. For example, in Great Britain for the period ending 24th May 2026, Non-Alcoholic Beverages recorded the highest inflation (+4.4%), followed by Confectionery & Snacks (+2.8%) and Frozen Food (+2.7%). In contrast, Homecare and Paper Products are in deflation (-1.1% and -0.9% respectively). Benjamin Cawthray, Client Director at NielsenIQ, said: “The first edition of the NIQ EU5 Inflation Barometer reveals a slowdown in FMCG inflation across Western Europe’s largest markets. By May 2026, EU5 FMCG inflation had slowed to +1.1%, reaching its lowest level of the year as pricing pressures eased across most markets . “While inflation is cooling at a regional level, the picture varies significantly by country. Great Britain remains the clear outlier, with FMCG inflation holding above 2%, while France has moved back into deflationary territory. Across continental Europe, a growing gap is emerging between FMCG inflation and broader consumer inflation, suggesting that supermarket pricing is no longer moving in line with wider economic trends. Shopper behaviour reflects these changing conditions. By analysing changes in promotional purchasing, retailer and brand choice, private label engagement, category participation and purchase volumes, the Barometer uncovers the key behaviours shaping FMCG growth across EU5 markets. This provides critical context to inflation trends, revealing how consumers are adapting their spending decisions in response to changing market conditions.” ” Notes to the Editor 1 NIQ Retailer Pricing Services Data; 13-week period ending May 24, 2026 vs. same period year ago. About NIQ EU5 Inflation Barometer The NIQ EU5 Inflation Barometer is based on harmonised FMCG retail measurement, consumer panel data and advanced analytics. It provides monthly analysis of inflation trends, shopper behaviour and price elasticity across France, Great Britain, Germany, Italy and Spain. For more information, please visit this page . About NIQ NielsenIQ (NYSE: NIQ) is a leading consumer intelligence company, delivering the most complete and trusted understanding of consumer buying behavior and revealing new pathways to growth. By combining an unmatched global data footprint and granular consumer and retail measurement with decades of AI modeling expertise, NIQ builds decision systems that help companies turn complex data into confident action. With operations in more than 90 countries, NIQ covers approximately 82% of the world’s population and more than $7.4 trillion in global consumer spend. Through cloud-based platforms, advanced analytics and AI-driven insights, NIQ delivers The Full View™—helping brands and retailers understand what consumers buy, why they buy it, and what to do next. title: What is ObjectiveFS?
summary: Explains what ObjectiveFS is and how it delivers a fully POSIX-compatible shared filesystem on top of object storage. Covers its architecture, consistency model, performance characteristics, and where it fits best for teams that need scalable, cloud-backed file storage without running a storage cluster.
body_text: Most teams that handle large amounts of data eventually run into the same tension: object storage scales beautifully, but it doesn’t behave like a real file system. Traditional NFS servers feel familiar, but they turn brittle and slow as workloads grow. Those two worlds rarely meet in the middle. ObjectiveFS was built to bridge that gap. No extra services to deploy, no databases, no Redis, and no fragile control plane to babysit. Instead, it provides a fully POSIX compatible file system backed directly by object storage, giving teams the semantics of a local file system with the scalability and durability of cloud-native object stores. ObjectiveFS is a shared filesystem for Linux and macOS that automatically scales up and out with high performance. Let’s unpack how it works and why so many engineering teams use it to scale without rewriting their applications. How ObjectiveFS Works ObjectiveFS takes a surprisingly straightforward approach to distributed storage. Your storage scales automatically with your workload and is accessible for reads and writes from all your machines. There’s no storage cluster to deploy or maintain. All you need is: ObjectiveFS running on your machines An object store such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or an on-premises equivalent Each client runs ObjectiveFS locally and communicates with the object store directly. This stateless design is one of its defining traits. Every node running ObjectiveFS maintains its own lightweight local cache for metadata and data, ensuring high performance without introducing additional infrastructure layers. The file system handles coordination internally, allowing multiple clients to read and write concurrently while maintaining file system consistency. Metadata and Data Placement Other cloud-backed file systems often rely on external datastores to track filenames, directory trees, permissions, etc. ObjectiveFS takes the approach of storing both your file data and metadata directly in the object store. This makes the system easier to reason about. The entire file system, the structure and content, lives in one place. Durability flows naturally from the object store, and because every node caches what it needs locally, day-to-day operations stay fast. It’s a clean model: a fully distributed system without the usual distributed-system baggage. Simplicity at Scale Most distributed storage systems come with a long list of operational tasks: cluster sizing, metadata tuning, periodic rebalancing, node health checks. ObjectiveFS avoids all of that. Once you install it, there’s rarely anything to maintain. Storage scales automatically because of the object store underneath. Throughput increases as you add more machines performing I/O operations. And failure scenarios are simple. If a node dies, the data is still safe, and any replacement machine can pick up where you left off. It fits neatly into cloud-native environments without acting like traditional infrastructure. POSIX Compatibility This is one of the main reasons teams adopt ObjectiveFS: it behaves exactly like a regular file system. Most modern and legacy applications assume POSIX semantics. They expect: permissions to behave in predictable ways file operations to be atomic directory hierarchies to exist commands like mv, chmod, and ln to just work ObjectiveFS supports all of that, which means you don’t need special SDKs or rewrites to adopt it. Your scripts work. Your applications work. Your workflows stay intact. It makes object storage feel familiar without forcing developers into REST APIs or object-store semantics. Consistency Across Clients and Regions When multiple machines write to the same directory hierarchy, keeping everything consistent is typically the hardest part of building a distributed file system. ObjectiveFS makes this almost invisible from the user’s perspective. All clients share a single view of the object store. When one machine writes a file or updates a directory, others pick up the change quickly. Because the object store acts as the single source of truth, this model scales naturally across availability zones and regions. For teams with globally distributed compute or parallel data-processing pipelines, this consistency model is particularly valuable. It removes the need for ad-hoc sync scripts or per-node caching hacks and gives teams a shared workspace that behaves predictably under load. Security That Adapts to Your Cloud ObjectiveFS doesn’t bolt on its own security system. Instead, it inherits the controls you already use in your cloud environment. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit, with key management handled by services like AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or Google Cloud KMS. Access is determined by IAM roles or object store credentials. Logging, monitoring, alerting, and further configurations flow through your cloud provider’s native tooling. Because of this, ObjectiveFS fits cleanly into compliance frameworks such as SOC 2, HIPAA, or ISO 27001. You’re not adopting a new trust model; you’re extending the one you already maintain. Performance and Reliability ObjectiveFS relies heavily on caching and parallel I/O to achieve strong performance. Frequently accessed files and directories are kept local, so your applications avoid unnecessary round-trips to the object store. When clients need to write large datasets, ObjectiveFS pushes them in parallel, letting throughput scale naturally with available network bandwidth. This architecture works well for workloads that favor large, sequential reads and writes, such as analytical jobs, media pipelines, or machine learning training. Small-file-heavy workloads benefit from caching and batching, but applications that require microsecond latency might prefer local SSDs or block-level storage. On the reliability side, ObjectiveFS relies on the durability SLA from the object store. If a machine goes offline, the data is still safe. New machines can mount the file system immediately, without waiting for data to rebuild or resync. Where ObjectiveFS Fits Best ObjectiveFS tends to excel in environments where teams want the convenience of a real file system without building a storage cluster. That includes: Machine Learning and AI workloads. Where shared training data needs to be accessed from multiple compute nodes with replication or synchronization overhead. Analytics and big-data pipelines. Where tools like Spark or Presto benefit from a POSIX layer backed by durable object storage. Containers. Where applications on Kubernetes or Docker need shared volumes that outlive compute nodes. Hybrid workloads. Where on-prem and cloud systems need access to the same data without custom transport layers. Backups. Workloads where scalable, durable storage is essential. ObjectiveFS won’t be ideal for every scenario. Single node transactional databases or ultra low latency systems will always favor block storage. ObjectiveFS vs Other Solutions There are plenty of ways to run file systems in the cloud, but each comes with tradeoffs: JuiceFS offers strong POSIX behavior too, but relies on external metadata engines (Redis, MySQL, etc) which introduces operational overhead. Cloud provider solutions like AWS EFS or FSx might introduce vendor lock-in and regional constraints. Goofys or S3FS make S3 feel more like a file system, but lack the consistency guarantees and POSIX compliance needed for real workloads. ObjectiveFS sidesteps all of these tradeoffs. It provides true file-system semantics, scales automatically with the underlying object store, and requires no additional services to operate. For teams that want shared, cloud-backed storage that “just works,” ObjectiveFS often ends up being the perfect fit. Final Thoughts ObjectiveFS gives teams a way to scale effortlessly while keeping the simplicity of a familiar file system. It turns object storage into something predictable and easy to work with, growing naturally alongside your workloads while avoiding the operational overhead that typically comes with distributed storage.

title: New Survey of 255 School-Based Therapists Reveals Rising Caseloads and Hidden Workload Threatening Student Access to Federally Mandated Services
summary: Kelly Pediatric Therapy surveyed 255 school-based therapists on rising caseloads and administrative burdens threatening student access to mandated services.
body_text: 71% of Therapists Report Caseload Growth in the Past Two Years; 77% Have Seen Student Progress Affected by Understaffing TROY, Mich., August 13, 2026 — Kelly Pediatric Therapy, a division of Kelly Education, today released The Hidden Workload Behind School-Based Pediatric Therapy , a new white paper based on original survey data from 255 school-based pediatric therapists across the United States. The findings document a profession under growing strain. Rising caseloads and the administrative work that follows therapists home are creating sustained pressure on both therapist sustainability and student outcomes. Among the key findings: 71% of therapists report their caseloads have grown in the past two years, with 24% describing that growth as significant. 77% of therapists have seen student progress affected by understaffing or unmanageable caseloads, with 39% saying this happens frequently or always. 68% of therapists spend six or more hours per week on documentation and IEP management outside contracted school hours. 64% say the complexity of student needs has increased over the past three years, with mental health and anxiety-related needs rising fastest. 57% of therapists believe school districts are not adequately prepared or are moving too slowly to address the coming therapist shortage. “School-based therapists are delivering federally mandated services inside systems that weren’t designed for clinical care,” said Cheryl Haibach, Vice President and Practice Lead, Kelly Pediatric Therapy. “What the data shows is that the caseload pressure and administrative demands those therapists are absorbing have reached the students depending on those services. This is happening now, and the districts investing in therapist retention and caseload structure are going to see the difference in student outcomes and service continuity.” The survey included speech-language pathologists, occupational therapists, physical therapists, school psychologists, and behavioral therapists working across public, private, and charter schools in all regions of the United States. Respondents represented both direct-hire and contracted employment arrangements. Eighty-seven percent of therapists say they feel at least somewhat supported by their districts, and nearly 90% remain at least somewhat optimistic about school-based practice as a long-term career. When asked what would most help them stay, therapists consistently ranked better therapy tools and spaces and manageable caseloads above compensation. The full white paper is available here . About Kelly Pediatric Therapy Kelly Pediatric Therapy delivers transformative pediatric therapeutic services across schools, early intervention programs, and outpatient centers. Founded in 1998 as Pediatric Therapeutic Services and acquired by Kelly (Nasdaq: KELYA, KELYB) in 2022, Kelly Pediatric Therapy connects children with experienced, caring therapists across occupational therapy, physical therapy, speech-language pathology, and behavioral health. Learn more at kellypediatrictherapy.com or connect with us on LinkedIn and Facebook .

title: How A Government CIO Shifted From Cost Cutting To Value
summary: Cost mandates usually trigger cuts. Our new case study describes how Patrick Newbold, CIO at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), spun a 2025 cost reduction mandate into a modernization opportunity. In doing so, he created a playbook that both public and private CIOs can leverage. Focus On Value, Not Cost CMS reframed […]
body_text: Cost mandates usually trigger cuts. Our new case study describes how Patrick Newbold , CIO at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) , spun a 2025 cost reduction mandate into a modernization opportunity. In doing so, he created a playbook that both public and private CIOs can leverage. Focus On Value, Not Cost CMS reframed the discussion from cost reduction to value optimization. Rather than asking what could be eliminated, Newbold focused on which investments best supported mission outcomes. This prevented reactive cuts and created a foundation for broader transformation. One example was platform consolidation. CMS reduced Atlassian instances from 16 to five and consolidated multiple Salesforce deployments into a single enterprise platform. The effort generated approximately $18 million in annualized savings while reducing operational complexity and security overhead. More importantly, those savings could be redirected toward modernization priorities. Turn Vendors Into Partners CMS also redefined its vendor relationships. Instead of focusing solely on contracts and deliverables, it asked vendors to work together as part of a larger ecosystem. For example, at CMS’s AI-focused Excite Day, leading product companies, systems integrators, and CMS’s internal teams partnered to educate, train, and guide staff in their practical application of AI tools. CMS was also transparent about financial realities. As a result, it was able to shift vendor compensation toward shared-value models aligned with outcomes that mattered to CMS’s mission. When the outcomes were exceeded, there were structured opportunities for scaled rewards. This encouraged vendors to consider how their solutions fit into CMS’s broader ecosystem and helped advance shared priorities and expected results. Build Trust Through Transparency Modernization requires trade-offs, and CMS chose to make those trade-offs explicit. Leaders consistently communicated priorities, constraints, and decision criteria, linking investment decisions to mission impact, affordability, security, and operational simplicity. That transparency reduced resistance to change and shifted accountability away from maintaining legacy systems and toward delivering measurable outcomes. And by applying this criteria consistently over time, CMS created a framework that reduced subjective or ad hoc decision-making. The Real Lesson The CMS story is about accepting constraints and leveraging them to drive better decisions. By establishing a culture rooted in the three principles of high-performance IT (alignment, adaptivity, and trust), CMS turned budget pressure into a catalyst for modernization, stronger partnerships, and more effective governance. title: 9 Questions for Choosing an AI EX Platform in 2026
summary: Choosing an AI EX platform in 2026? Ask these 9 critical questions to evaluate AI capabilities, integrations, employee adoption, security, and ROI.
body_text: Question 1: Does the Platform Integrate With Your Existing HR Technology Stack? Integration capabilities determine whether an AI employee experience platform becomes part of your workflow or creates another data silo. You need to understand how the platform connects with your existing HRIS, payroll systems, performance management tools and collaboration platforms before you evaluate features. Native Connectors vs. Custom APIs Native integrations come pre-built into the software and allow direct communication between applications without third-party tools. These integrations activate through simple settings within your HR technology stack. They're economical since licensing fees cover them. Most platforms offer native integrations for common services like Salesforce, Zoom and Microsoft 365. Custom API integration involves building tailored connections from scratch using API code developed independently. Native options work for standard processes. Custom APIs excel when you need unique data transformations or must connect legacy systems that lack modern API support. Companies using APIs report being 24% more likely to succeed. Integrations boost customer satisfaction by 20% and reduce operational costs by 15%. The trade-off centers on flexibility versus implementation speed. Native integrations deploy within hours. Custom API development spans 4-8 weeks. Native connectors handle most requirements for mid-sized technology companies at first. Custom development becomes necessary when proprietary systems or specialized workflows enter the picture. Single Sign-On and Authentication Single sign-on eliminates password fatigue by allowing employees to access multiple applications with one set of credentials. SSO implementations reduce login-related help desk calls by 75% and enable users to adopt new applications 50% faster, according to industry research. This simplified access proves essential for distributed engineering teams working across time zones. SSO implementations rely on several authentication protocols. SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) provides greater security control and works well for enterprise or government domains. OAuth makes simplified interactions between applications possible without exposing passwords. OpenID Connect layers on top of OAuth for social logins and lighter-weight implementations across SaaS applications. LDAP defines directories for storing user credentials and remains the authentication solution of choice for organizations requiring granular access control. Platform vendors offering over 8,000 pre-built integrations eliminate custom code requirements and ongoing maintenance burdens. This breadth matters when your tech stack has specialized tools or industry-specific applications. Two-factor or multi-factor authentication should complement any SSO implementation. Requiring additional authentication factors like mobile codes or fingerprints reduces risks related to compromised credentials, even with long, complex passwords encrypted and protected. Data Flow and Synchronization Data synchronization keeps employee information consistent across systems without manual intervention. Live synchronization updates data within seconds, which proves critical for inventory management in HR tech contexts or live dashboards monitoring employee engagement. Near-live synchronization operates with latency measured in seconds to minutes and balances freshness with reduced infrastructure complexity. Change data capture identifies and transfers only modified data since the last sync. This minimizes the effect on system performance. CDC reads transaction logs rather than querying tables directly, making it the preferred method for syncing operational databases when freshness requirements fall under a few minutes. Unified workforce data becomes non-negotiable for AI-powered HR technology platforms. AI hallucination rates rise and workflow automation stalls when employee skills profiles, performance history, learning engagement and career trajectory exist across disconnected systems. Fragmented data prevents the context AI requires to move from isolated insights to automated action. Platforms polling data sources as often as every five minutes provide near-live feeds, though capabilities may vary based on data volume and vendor plan types. The synchronization approach you select affects whether your employee experience software delivers current insights or operates on stale information that undermines decision-making. Question 2: What AI Capabilities Does the Platform Actually Offer? Image Source: IBM Vendors claim their platforms use "AI-powered insights" or "intelligent automation," but these terms mask wide variations in actual capability. What AI features exist beneath the marketing language determines whether you gain genuine predictive power or just glorified reporting dashboards. Predictive Analytics for Employee Retention Predictive models identify employees at risk of leaving before traditional signals like exit interviews reveal the problem. Machine learning algorithms analyze historical turnover patterns, engagement scores, tenure data and performance metrics to calculate flight risk scores. XGBoost delivers the strongest performance for turnover prediction. Research comparing multiple algorithms showed XGBoost achieved an AUC of 0.95 in specific organizational contexts and 0.86 across general studies. Random Forest models reached accuracy rates between 91.76% and 100% depending on feature selection and data quality. Decision trees demonstrated 98% accuracy in employee retention prediction tasks. The performance gap between algorithms matters. SVM models achieved only 0.72 AUC in some implementations. Logistic regression ranged from 0.70 to 0.85. Neural networks captured complex patterns with AUC scores between 0.84 and 0.92, though they require larger datasets and longer training periods. Model accuracy changes with balancing techniques. ADASYN oversampling improved F1 scores from 0.503 on imbalanced data to between 0.91 and 0.93. Feature selection using Pearson correlation reduced redundancy and increased efficiency without sacrificing predictive power. Generative AI for Personalized Engagement Generative AI creates customized learning paths, career development plans and communication strategies tailored to individual employee profiles. The 2ACT framework uses natural language processing to analyze skill gaps and labor market trends. It generates personalized learning paths that bridge current positions and future career objectives. AI-driven HRM models integrate live feedback mechanisms, behavioral monitoring and adaptive recommendations for training and internal mobility. These systems detect early signs of burnout, disengagement or professional stagnation and respond with personalized suggestions based on contextual data and psychosocial indicators. AI Employee Assistant Features AI assistants automate repetitive workflows, organize data, summarize insights and answer predefined questions using machine learning and natural language processing. Workers save 97 minutes per week on average by using available AI features, according to internal analysis. Daily AI use increased 233% in just six months among global desk workers surveyed in June 2025. These assistants make tasks like scheduling meetings, creating meeting summaries and highlighting action items more efficient. Slack AI's search feature uses natural language prompts to scan channels and threads for key insights. This enables faster information retrieval. AI can track milestones and provide live updates to stakeholders for project management, keeping teams informed between meetings. Agentic Automation and Workflow Intelligence Agentic AI operates autonomously. It reasons through complex multi-step tasks and adapts to dynamic situations without constant human intervention. This capability moves beyond automation into orchestration across HRIS, payroll and IT systems. UiPath reports that 75% of large enterprises will use AI-powered talent intelligence platforms to support hiring decisions by 2025. Organizations implementing agentic automation see 60-70% less time spent on automated administrative work. Recruiters using AI-powered tools experience an 80% reduction in manual work, allowing focus on strategic tasks. Agentic systems handle end-to-end processes like onboarding, where they coordinate tasks across HR, IT and facilities without manual handoffs. These platforms interpret manager requests and match them to correct system modules. They execute them in mandated order while ensuring compliance. Question 3: How Does the Platform Handle Employee Data Privacy and Security? Image Source: Moveworks Employee data processed by AI employee experience platforms falls under strict regulatory scrutiny. The platform you select must demonstrate compliance frameworks that protect sensitive information while maintaining operational functionality in your distributed engineering teams. Compliance With Global Privacy Regulations GDPR compliance requires AI-powered HR technology to establish valid legal bases for processing employee data . Consent rarely works in employment relationships due to the inherent power imbalance between employers and employees. Workers cannot refuse data collection without fear of repercussions. This makes them a "captive population" regarding workplace technologies. Platforms should rely on contractual necessity, legal obligation, or legitimate interest as processing grounds instead. GDPR requires that consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. The withdrawal process must remain as easy as giving consent. Platforms that collect special categories of data like health information or biometric data for benefits or access control require stronger legal bases and additional technical safeguards. CCPA grants California employees rights to know what personal information gets collected, request deletion and correct inaccuracies for workforce engagement platforms operating around the world. HIPAA applies when platforms sponsor health plans or wellness programs that collect employee medical data. China's PIPL requires explicit consent before processing employee data and regulates cross-border transfers, often requiring government approval. Non-compliance carries severe penalties. GDPR fines reach up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover. The Hamburg Data Protection Authority fined H&M €35.3 million in 2020 for surveilling employees without authorization. The company collected detailed personal information about family issues, religious beliefs and medical histories without knowledge or consent. Data Encryption and Access Controls Encryption transforms data into formats readable only with correct decryption keys. Platforms should encrypt employee data both at rest and in transit to prevent unauthorized access. AES-256 encryption provides maximum security for stored databases, while TLS 1.3 protocols secure web-based interactions. Access control determines who can view employee information. Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions based on job functions. HR assistants access contact information but not salary data, while payroll administrators see compensation details but not performance reviews. Multi-factor authentication reduces risks even when passwords become compromised. Platforms processing employee data must respond to breach notifications within 72 hours under GDPR requirements. Organizations lacking formal data breach response plans face higher exposure, with 77% of organizations lacking such plans . Transparency and Employee Consent Mechanisms Employees must understand what data gets collected, why platforms use it and who accesses it. Privacy notices should explain processing activities in plain language, including how AI systems handle personal data. Transparency becomes especially important when AI influences hiring, promotion or performance decisions because 71% of Americans oppose AI making final hiring decisions. Platforms should enable employees to request access to their data, correct inaccuracies and understand automated decision-making logic. GDPR gives employees the right to challenge automated decisions that affect their employment. Question 4: What Are the Total Costs Beyond the Base Subscription? Image Source: Monday.com Subscription pricing rarely tells the full financial story. Mid-sized technology companies evaluating AI-powered HR technology must account for implementation fees, AI usage charges, and ongoing costs that revolutionize advertised rates into actual expenditure. Per-Employee Pricing vs. Usage-Based Models Per-employee-per-month (PEPM) pricing charges a flat fee for each registered employee. monday service runs INR 2,193.89 per seat monthly on Standard and INR 3,206.46 on Pro, with 18% discounts for annual prepayment. ServiceNow and Workday use quote-based PEPM structures customized by scope and user count. Usage-based models arrange costs with consumption. Zendesk charges INR 126.57 per automated resolution on committed plans or INR 168.76 pay-as-you-go. Intercom bills INR 83.54 per resolution for Fin. 72% of HR software buyers prefer pricing that matches actual usage over fixed rates. Consumption-based pricing eliminates shelfware risk. PEPM models see adoption rates hover between 20% and 40%. Organizations pay for 10,000 seats but extract value from 2,000 to 4,000. Consumption models start low and scale with showed value. Costs rise only when usage increases. Implementation and Onboarding Costs Deployment timelines affect project costs. Platforms like monday service and Fini ship in 48 hours. Userpilot and Appcues deploy within 1-2 weeks. Pendo requires 2-3 months, while WalkMe stretches 8-16 weeks. Implementation fees vary. Enterprise platforms like ServiceNow and Pendo start between INR 2,109,511.27 and INR 4,219,022.54 annually . Custom Workday integrations cost INR 4,219,022.54 to INR 8,438,045.08 without pre-built connectors. First-year setup has data migration and customization, along with project management. Hidden Costs of AI Feature Add-Ons AI capabilities require separate entitlements. Zendesk AI Copilot adds INR 4,219.02 per agent monthly. Freshservice restricts Freddy AI Insights to Enterprise tier, with 1,200 AI Agent sessions included annually. Microsoft Viva charges INR 506.28 per user monthly for workplace analytics, with Copilot features that need additional licensing. Guardian security add-ons and advanced compliance modules introduce costs beyond base subscriptions. ROI Calculation Framework Calculate total cost of ownership across three years. This should include licenses and implementation, along with hidden adoption costs. Organizations using consumption-based HR technology report 30-45% lower TCO compared to per-seat models. Most platforms achieve positive ROI within 3-6 months and average 340% returns within 18 months. Time savings reach 14-20 hours weekly per HR professional. This translates to over INR 1,518,848.11 in annual savings. Question 5: Can the Platform Scale for Distributed Engineering Teams? Image Source: eXo Platform Geographic distribution introduces operational complexity that base features don't address very well. AI employee experience platforms built for single-location teams struggle when engineering staff spans continents. They need specialized capabilities for time zones, work models, and language barriers. Multi-Location and Time Zone Support Distributed teams face scheduling friction that compounds each day. By 2026, 72% of companies have team members working in multiple time zones. Coordinating a single meeting from New York to London and Tokyo requires an average of 17 minutes of back-and-forth communication. Five participants in four time zones share only 0-2 hours of overlapping working hours. Daylight Saving Time amplifies this complexity. More than 70 countries observe DST, but transition dates vary by region. Every cross-timezone meeting risks incorrect scheduling for 2-3 weeks twice a year as gaps between zones move. A Monday 3 PM ET / 8 PM GMT call works in January, but the same meeting becomes 3 PM EDT / 7 PM GMT when the US springs forward in March before the UK—an hour earlier for London participants. Workforce engagement platforms need automated timezone detection from calendar settings and up-to-the-minute conversion that displays each participant's local time. They must also provide proactive DST adjustment before transitions occur. Multi-timezone applications must handle users and data sources located in different timezones where time of day remains relevant to information handled. Remote and Hybrid Work Features Hybrid-remote models blend in-office and remote work through three main structures. Flexible hybrid allows employees to change location and working hours based on workload needs. This freedom increases loyalty and job satisfaction. Fixed hybrid sets specific days and times for remote or office work. This makes in-person meetings easier to schedule ahead but may reduce productivity for employees needing focus time. Office-first models expect employees in the office most of the week with optional remote days, while remote-first reverses this arrangement. Employee experience software must accommodate these variations. More than half (55%) of U.S. employees prefer working remotely at least three days weekly, while 83% of employers report successful remote work transitions. Language and Localization Capabilities Multi-country HR systems require native language translations at no extra charge. Platforms like Cezanne HR provide Greek, Dutch, German, French, US English, Romanian, and Turkish translations made by native speakers. All translations update at the same time as new features ship. Date and currency formatting must adapt to regional needs. UK employees select dd/mm/yy format while US staff choose mm/dd/yy. Salaries display in local currencies but associate with preferred base currencies for cross-organization comparisons. Double-byte character sets supporting Chinese, Japanese, and Greek prove critical for tracking employees' legal names. Question 6: How Effective Are the Workforce Engagement Tools? Image Source: MangoApps Measuring engagement requires tools that capture employees' sentiment with precision and respond quickly. The gap between claimed engagement features and actual effect separates platforms that boost retention from those that generate unused dashboards. Pulse Surveys and Immediate Feedback Pulse surveys deliver short, focused questionnaires that track specific workplace conditions between annual engagement studies. They work best when conducted after organizational changes like leadership transitions, job restructuring, or team composition moves. The golden rule: only gather feedback as often as you can act on it. Employee response rates increase when action follows survey results and decline when no change occurs. Effective pulse surveys limit questions to 5-15 items completable within minutes. Weekly surveys prove unsustainable and yield inaccurate responses as employees receive similar questions over and over. Pulse surveys excel at tracking perception changes over time and measuring action plan effectiveness while maintaining early warning systems for business metrics like safety or customer service. Recognition and Rewards Integration Recognition platforms enable peer-to-peer acknowledgment and manager-led awards through centralized systems. Employees who receive meaningful feedback are almost four times more likely to be engaged. 92% of companies that use recognition software reported reduced burnout, while 98% achieved peer recognition rates. Platforms like Bonusly, Achievers, and Workhuman aid immediate recognition through e-cards, badges, and awards while integrating with HR systems to automate tracking. HiFives uses AI-driven prompts and Kaizen modules with deep workflow integration for Teams, Slack, and WhatsApp. Advantage Club emphasizes agentic AI for emotionally intelligent employee experiences through automated tasks and personalized nudges. Career Development and Learning Pathways Career pathing provides employees with clearly defined strategies to build skills, master current roles, and qualify for promotions. Organizations that implement career pathing experience 34% higher retention rates than those without structured development. Employees are 76% more likely to stay with companies offering continuous training. Learning pathways curate content that guides learners through strong development experiences and connects material relevant to related skill sets or career trajectories. These pathways enable L&D teams to scale individual development for 500 employees managing 500 unique development plans. Employee Sentiment Analysis Sentiment analysis uses natural language processing, AI, and machine learning to analyze employee comments, feedback, and unstructured data. This technology interprets qualitative data with the same weight as quantitative metrics and highlights company strengths, weaknesses, and sentiment toward policies or culture changes. Organizations that use AI-driven sentiment analysis spot disengagement 40% faster than those relying on manual reviews. Question 7: What Analytics and Reporting Capabilities Are Included? Image Source: inFeedo AI Reporting depth separates platforms that surface useful intelligence from those that bury HR teams in raw data exports. AI-powered HR technology must translate workforce information into strategic intelligence that informs retention decisions, staffing models and resource allocation. Customizable Dashboards for HR Leaders Modern workforce engagement platforms provide interactive dashboards where HR professionals build tailored views without coding experience. Drag-and-drop functionality allows teams to arrange visualizations that track headcount trends, turnover analysis, diversity breakdowns, hiring velocity and employee engagement scores . Live data integration ensures dashboards reflect current workforce conditions rather than outdated snapshots. Mobile optimization enables access from any device. Platforms like Tableau offer executive HR dashboards that display high-level metrics such as employees by role and location alongside key ratios for gender and training. Predictive Turnover and Retention Insights Flight risk models analyze engagement surveys, demographic details, performance ratings and past turnover data to pinpoint employees who show early signs of disengagement. These systems flag at-risk employee groups and reveal critical intelligence through advanced search capabilities. Research shows that organizations using AI-driven predictive analytics identify employees 40% faster than manual review processes. This enables timely interventions before top talent departs. Standard Data for Mid-Sized Technology Companies Industry standards provide context for internal metrics. The Hackett Group's AI World Class HR research quantifies how process-led AI transformation delivers recruiting costs per hire declining by up to 61% , recruiter productivity improving by up to 119% and time-to-fill decreasing by up to 57%. These standards draw from organizations including 98% of Dow Jones Global Titans, 97% of Dow Jones Industrials and 90% of Fortune 100 companies. For staffing comparisons, private companies with fewer than 1,000 employees maintain a median of 38 full-time employees per HR team member. Exportable Reports and Data Portability Platforms must support data export in common formats including PDF, PNG and Excel for presentations and compliance documentation. Secure sharing capabilities allow HR leaders to distribute tailored dashboards to executives and department managers based on defined permissions while maintaining confidentiality. Question 8: What Is Your Exit Strategy If the Platform Doesn't Work? Image Source: LinkedIn You need to anticipate failure scenarios before they occur when you select an AI employee experience platform. Most mid-sized technology companies focus on features during procurement but overlook how they'll extract themselves when vendor relationships deteriorate or business requirements move. Data Export and Migration Support HR data migration just needs standard migration tools from vendors to minimize custom coding effort. Organizations lacking these tools face substantially higher migration costs and extended timelines. Platforms should provide data export in CSV, JSON, or XML formats that competing systems accept. SAP SuccessFactors has standard migration tools for employee master and organizational data as part of subscription fees. Migration handbooks organized by project phases reduce implementation risks. Contract Terms and Cancelation Policies Cancelation clauses specify exit conditions, notice requirements and financial penalties before contract expiration. Notice periods usually span 30 to 90 days, though timing calculations vary by vendor. Some platforms calculate notice from billing cycles rather than submission dates and create unexpected delays. California's Automatic Renewal Law requires clear disclosure of auto-renewal terms and simple cancelation methods for consumer subscriptions. Vendor Lock-In Risks Vendor lock-in occurs when switching costs exceed the benefits of migration. The European Commission recognizes vendor lock-in as one of the greatest obstacles to enterprise cloud adoption. Proprietary data formats and custom APIs create switching barriers. Organizations should select vendors supporting standardized formats and protocols regarding data structures and APIs. Question 9: How Does the Platform Support Adoption and Change Management? Image Source: Ventana Research - ISG Technology purchases fail when adoption lags. This makes post-sale support infrastructure as critical as feature sets. Employee experience platforms succeed when vendors provide structured training, responsive support and realistic implementation roadmaps that account for organizational change resistance. Training Resources for HR Teams and Employees Platforms that offer free and unlimited training eliminate ongoing education costs. AI literacy workshops span executives, operational staff and technical teams to accelerate adoption. Companies that invest in cultural change achieve 5.3× higher success rates . Role-based training ensures HR assistants and managers understand relevant platform sections without overwhelming them with unnecessary features. Customer Support and Response Times Response speed influences trust and adoption rates. While 62% of businesses never respond to support emails, employees expect replies within 4 hours. Platforms that monitor support channels Monday through Friday, 9 AM to 5 PM, provide baseline accessibility. First response time under 1 hour associates with sustained platform usage. Delays trigger workarounds that undermine adoption. Community and User Resources Self-service knowledge bases reduce support ticket volume. They enable employees to resolve queries on their own. Help center articles, troubleshooting guides and FAQs encourage employee autonomy while freeing support teams for complex issues. Implementation Timeline and Milestones Deployment spans 6-8 weeks for focused implementations versus 14-28 months for enterprise builds. Phases have discovery (2-4 weeks), data preparation (2 weeks), pilot build (4-8 weeks) and production deployment. Organizations that bring clean data sources, dedicated evaluation set owners and executive support compress timelines by 4-6 months.
